109+-- ## Decorated Programs
110+
111+-- The beauty of Hoare Logic is that it is *syntax directed*: the structure of
112+-- proofs exactly follows the structure of programs.
113+
114+-- We can record the essential ideas of a Hoare-logic proof — omitting
115+-- low-level calculational details — by "decorating" a program with
116+-- appropriate assertions on each of its commands.
117+
118+-- Such a *decorated program* carries within itself an argument for its own
119+-- correctness.
120+
121+-- For example, consider the program:
122+
123+--   X := m;
124+--   Z := p;
125+--   while X <> 0 do
126+--     Z := Z - 1;
127+--     X := X - 1
128+--   end
129+
130+-- Here is one possible specification for this program, in the form of a Hoare
131+-- triple:
132+
133+--   {{ True }}
134+--   X := m;
135+--   Z := p;
136+--   while X <> 0 do
137+--     Z := Z - 1;
138+--     X := X - 1
139+--   end
140+--   {{ Z = p - m }}
141+
142+-- (Note the *parameters* `m` and `p`, which stand for fixed-but-arbitrary
143+-- numbers. Formally, they are simply Lean variables of type `Nat`.)
144+
145+-- Here is a decorated version of this program, embodying a proof of this
146+-- specification:
147+
148+--   {{ True }} ->>
149+--   {{ m = m }}
150+--     X := m
151+--                        {{ X = m }} ->>
152+--                        {{ X = m /\ p = p }};
153+--     Z := p;
154+--                        {{ X = m /\ Z = p }} ->>
155+--                        {{ Z - X = p - m }}
156+--     while X <> 0 do
157+--                        {{ Z - X = p - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
158+--                        {{ (Z - 1) - (X - 1) = p - m }}
159+--       Z := Z - 1
160+--                        {{ Z - (X - 1) = p - m }};
161+--       X := X - 1
162+--                        {{ Z - X = p - m }}
163+--     end
164+--   {{ Z - X = p - m /\ ~ (X <> 0) }} ->>
165+--   {{ Z = p - m }}
166+
167+-- Note to developers:
168+--     `HIDE: MRC'20: It bothers me a little in the proof above (and
169+--     similarly throughout the whole file really when it comes to guards)
170+--     that when we get to this part:
171+--     [[
172+--      while X <> 0 do {{ Z - X = p - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
173+--     ]]
174+--     we are inconsistent about [X <> 0] vs. [~(X=0)].  I admit they
175+--     evaluate the same (er, sort of---the former is a [bexp] whereas the
176+--     latter is an assertion), but they aren't syntactically the same.
177+--     Since what we're teaching here (mechanized Hoare logic) is fussy
178+--     about syntax, it strikes me as something we ought to be precise
179+--     about. But it's an annoying change to propagate through the file,
180+--     so I haven't done it. Is it worth a comment, or do others not get
181+--     bothered by this?  Another way to fix this would be to add the [<>]
182+--     operator to Imp, so that we can write the guard in the nicer way.
183+--
184+--     BCP 20: I think adding in a few more boolean operators at the
185+--     outside is the way to go...
186+--
187+--     BCP 21: ... and I've now done this: <> is available in formal
188+--     bexps (also >).`
189+
190+-- Concretely, a decorated program consists of the program's text interleaved
191+-- with assertions (sometimes multiple assertions separated by ->>).
192+
193+-- A decorated program can be viewed as a compact representation of a proof in
194+-- Hoare Logic: the assertions surrounding each command specify the Hoare
195+-- triple to be proved for that part of the program using one of the Hoare
196+-- Logic rules, and the structure of the program itself shows how to assemble
197+-- all these individual steps into a proof for the whole program.
198+
199+-- Our goal is to verify such decorated programs "mostly automatically." But,
200+-- before we can verify anything, we need to be able to *find* a proof for a
201+-- given specification, and for this we need to discover the right assertions.
202+-- This can be done in an almost mechanical way, with the exception of finding
203+-- loop invariants. In the remainder of this section, we explain in detail how
204+-- to construct decorations for several short programs, all of which are loop
205+-- free or have simple loop invariants. We'll return to finding more
206+-- interesting loop invariants later in the chapter.
207+
208+-- ### Example: Swapping
209+
210+-- Consider the following program, which swaps the values of two variables
211+-- using addition and subtraction, instead of by assigning to a temporary
212+-- variable.
213+
214+--   X := X + Y;
215+--   Y := X - Y;
216+--   X := X - Y
217+
218+-- We can give a proof, in the form of decorations, that this program is
219+-- correct — i.e., it really swaps `X` and `Y` — as follows.
220+
221+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>
222+--   (2)    {{ (X + Y) - ((X + Y) - Y) = n /\ (X + Y) - Y = m }}
223+--            X := X + Y
224+--   (3)                     {{ X - (X - Y) = n /\ X - Y = m }};
225+--            Y := X - Y
226+--   (4)                     {{ X - Y = n /\ Y = m }};
227+--            X := X - Y
228+--   (5)    {{ X = n /\ Y = m }}
229+
230+-- The decorations can be constructed as follows:
231+
232+-- - We begin with the undecorated program (the unnumbered lines).
233+
234+-- - We add the specification — i.e., the outer precondition (1) and
235+--   postcondition (5). In the precondition, we use parameters `m` and `n` to
236+--   remember the initial values of variables `X` and `Y` so that we can refer
237+--   to them in the postcondition (5).
238+
239+-- - We work backwards, mechanically, starting from (5) and proceeding until we
240+--   get to (2). At each step, we obtain the precondition of the assignment from
241+--   its postcondition by substituting the assigned variable with the
242+--   right-hand-side of the assignment. For instance, we obtain (4) by
243+--   substituting `X` with `X - Y` in (5), and we obtain (3) by substituting `Y`
244+--   with `X - Y` in (4).
245+
246+-- - Finally, we verify that (1) logically implies (2) — i.e., that the step
247+--   from (1) to (2) is a valid use of the law of consequence — by doing a bit
248+--   of high-school algebra.
249+
250+-- Note to developers:
251+--     HIDE: BCP 21: This side comment seems too technical:
252+--
253+--     - (Note that we are working with natural numbers rather than fixed-width
254+--       machine integers, so we don't need to worry about the possibility of
255+--       arithmetic overflow anywhere in this argument. This makes life quite a
256+--       bit simpler!)
257+--
258+--     HIDE: A quick / optional exercise using just assignment here would be
259+--     good.
260+
261+-- ### Example: Simple Conditionals
262+
263+-- Here is a simple decorated program using conditionals:
264+
265+--   (1)   {{ True }}
266+--           if X <= Y then
267+--   (2)                    {{ True /\ X <= Y }} ->>
268+--   (3)                    {{ (Y - X) + X = Y \/ (Y - X) + Y = X }}
269+--             Z := Y - X
270+--   (4)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
271+--           else
272+--   (5)                    {{ True /\ ~(X <= Y) }} ->>
273+--   (6)                    {{ (X - Y) + X = Y \/ (X - Y) + Y = X }}
274+--             Z := X - Y
275+--   (7)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
276+--           end
277+--   (8)   {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
278+
279+-- These decorations can be constructed as follows:
280+
281+-- - We start with the outer precondition (1) and postcondition (8).
282+
283+-- - Following the format dictated by the `hoare_if` rule, we copy the
284+--   postcondition (8) to (4) and (7). We conjoin the precondition (1) with the
285+--   guard of the conditional to obtain (2). We conjoin (1) with the negated
286+--   guard of the conditional to obtain (5).
287+
288+-- - In order to use the assignment rule and obtain (3), we substitute `Z` by
289+--   `Y - X` in (4). To obtain (6) we substitute `Z` by `X - Y` in (7).
290+
291+-- - Finally, we verify that (2) implies (3) and (5) implies (6). Both of these
292+--   implications crucially depend on the ordering of `X` and `Y` obtained from
293+--   the guard. For instance, knowing that `X <= Y` ensures that subtracting `X`
294+--   from `Y` and then adding back `X` produces `Y`, as required by the first
295+--   disjunct of (3). Similarly, knowing that `~ (X <= Y)` ensures that
296+--   subtracting `Y` from `X` and then adding back `Y` produces `X`, as needed
297+--   by the second disjunct of (6). Note that `n - m + m = n` does *not* hold
298+--   for arbitrary natural numbers `n` and `m` (for example, [3 - 5 + 5 = 5]).
299+
300+-- Note to developers:
301+--     NOTATION: LATER: The `~` in that paragraph will typeset wrong if the
302+--     space after it is removed. Maybe it's better to give up on all the
303+--     unicode hacks in the generated HTML...?
304+
305+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): if_minus_plus_reloaded (manually graded) ⭐⭐
306+
307+-- N.b.: Although this exercise is marked optional, it is an excellent warm-up
308+-- for the (non-optional) `if_minus_plus_correct` exercise below!
309+
310+-- Fill in valid decorations for the following program:
311+
312+--   {{ True }}
313+--     if X <= Y then
314+--               {{                         }} ->>
315+--               {{                         }}
316+--       Z := Y - X
317+--               {{                         }}
318+--     else
319+--               {{                         }} ->>
320+--               {{                         }}
321+--       Y := X + Z
322+--               {{                         }}
323+--     end
324+--   {{ Y = X + Z }}
325+
326+-- Briefly justify each use of `->>`.
327+
328+--   {{ True }}
329+--     if X <= Y then
330+--          {{ True /\ X <= Y }} ->>
331+--          {{ Y = X + (Y - X) }}
332+--       Z := Y - X
333+--          {{ Y = X + Z }}
334+--     else
335+--          {{ True /\ ~(X <= Y) }} ->>
336+--          {{ X + Z = X + Z }}
337+--       Y := X + Z
338+--          {{ Y = X + Z }}
339+--     end
340+--   {{ Y = X + Z }}
341+
342+-- The second use of consequence is trivial, while the first crucially depends
343+-- on the `X <= Y` condition, which ensures that subtracting `X` from `Y` and
344+-- then adding back `X` produces `Y`.
345+
346+-- ### Example: Reduce to Zero
347+
348+-- Here is a `while` loop that is so simple that `True` suffices as a loop
349+-- invariant.
350+
351+--   (1)    {{ True }}
352+--            while X <> 0 do
353+--   (2)                  {{ True /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
354+--   (3)                  {{ True }}
355+--              X := X - 1
356+--   (4)                  {{ True }}
357+--            end
358+--   (5)    {{ True /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>
359+--   (6)    {{ X = 0 }}
360+
361+-- The decorations can be constructed as follows:
362+
363+-- - Start with the outer precondition (1) and postcondition (6).
364+
365+-- - Following the format dictated by the `hoare_while` rule, we copy (1) to
366+--   (4). We conjoin (1) with the guard to obtain (2). We also conjoin (1) with
367+--   the negation of the guard to obtain (5).
368+
369+-- - Because the final postcondition (6) does not syntactically match (5), we
370+--   add an implication between them.
371+
372+-- - Using the assignment rule with assertion (4), we trivially substitute and
373+--   obtain assertion (3).
374+
375+-- - We add the implication between (2) and (3).
376+
377+-- Finally we check that the implications do hold; both are trivial.
378+
379+-- ### Example: Division
380+
381+-- Let's do one more example of simple reasoning about a loop.
382+
383+-- The following Imp program calculates the integer quotient and remainder of
384+-- parameters `m` and `n`.
385+
386+--   X := m;
387+--   Y := 0;
388+--   while n <= X do
389+--     X := X - n;
390+--     Y := Y + 1
391+--   end;
392+
393+-- If we replace `m` and `n` by concrete numbers and execute the program, it
394+-- will terminate with the variable `X` set to the remainder when `m` is
395+-- divided by `n` and `Y` set to the quotient.
396+
397+-- In order to give a specification to this program we need to remember that
398+-- dividing `m` by `n` produces a remainder `X` and a quotient `Y` such that
399+-- `n * Y + X = m /\ X < n`.
400+
401+-- It turns out that we get lucky with this program and don't have to think
402+-- very hard about the loop invariant: the loop invariant is just the first
403+-- conjunct, `n * Y + X = m`, and we can use this to decorate the program.
404+
405+--    (1)  {{ True }} ->>
406+--    (2)  {{ n * 0 + m = m }}
407+--           X := m;
408+--    (3)                     {{ n * 0 + X = m }}
409+--           Y := 0;
410+--    (4)                     {{ n * Y + X = m }}
411+--           while n <= X do
412+--    (5)                     {{ n * Y + X = m /\ n <= X }} ->>
413+--    (6)                     {{ n * (Y + 1) + (X - n) = m }}
414+--             X := X - n;
415+--    (7)                     {{ n * (Y + 1) + X = m }}
416+--             Y := Y + 1
417+--    (8)                     {{ n * Y + X = m }}
418+--           end
419+--    (9)  {{ n * Y + X = m /\ ~ (n <= X) }} ->>
420+--   (10)  {{ n * Y + X = m /\ X < n }}
421+
422+-- Assertions (4), (5), (8), and (9) are derived mechanically from the loop
423+-- invariant and the loop's guard. Assertions (8), (7), and (6) are derived
424+-- using the assignment rule going backwards from (8) to (6). Assertions (4),
425+-- (3), and (2) are again backwards applications of the assignment rule.
426+
427+-- Now that we've decorated the program it only remains to check that the uses
428+-- of the consequence rule are correct — i.e., that (1) implies (2), that (5)
429+-- implies (6), and that (9) implies (10). This is indeed the case:
430+
431+-- - (1) ->> (2): trivial, by algebra.
432+
433+-- - (5) ->> (6): because `n <= X`, we are guaranteed that the subtraction in
434+--   (6) does not get zero-truncated. We can therefore rewrite (6) as
435+--   `n * Y + n + X - n` and cancel the `n`s, which results in the left conjunct
436+--   of (5).
437+
438+-- - (9) ->> (10): if `~ (n <= X)` then `X < n`. That's straightforward from
439+--   high-school algebra. So, we have a valid decorated program.
440+
441+-- ### From Decorated Programs to Formal Proofs
442+
443+-- From an informal proof in the form of a decorated program, it is "easy in
444+-- principle" to read off a formal proof using the Lean theorems corresponding
445+-- to the Hoare Logic rules, but these proofs can be a bit long and fiddly.
446+
447+-- Note that we do *not* unfold the definition of `ValidHoareTriple` anywhere
448+-- in this proof: the point of the game we're playing now is to use the Hoare
449+-- rules as a self-contained logic for reasoning about programs.
450+
451+-- For example...
452+
453+def reduceToZero : Com :=
454+  imp {
455+    while (X ≠ 0) {
456+      X := X - 1;
457+    }
458+  }
459+
460+theorem reduce_to_zero_correct' :
461+    {{ True }} ~reduceToZero {{ X = 0 }} := by
462+  -- First put the postcondition into the form expected by
463+  -- the while rule.
464+  sorry
465+
466+-- In Hoare we introduced a series of tactics named `assertion_auto` to
467+-- automate proofs involving assertions.
468+
469+-- The following declaration introduces a more sophisticated tactic that will
470+-- help with proving assertions throughout the rest of this chapter. You don't
471+-- need to understand the details, but briefly: it introduces the available
472+-- hypotheses, simplifies assertions, maps, and arithmetic expressions, and
473+-- then asks `lia` to solve linear arithmetic goals. What's left after
474+-- `verify_assertion` does its work should be just the "interesting parts" of
475+-- the proof (which, if we're lucky, might be nothing at all!).
476+
477+macro "verify_assertion" : tactic =>
478+  `(tactic| assertion_auto')
479+
480+-- This makes it pretty easy to verify `reduce_to_zero`:
481+
482+theorem reduce_to_zero_correct''' :
483+    {{ True }} ~reduceToZero {{ X = 0 }} := by
484+  sorry
485+
486+-- This example shows that it is conceptually straightforward to read off the
487+-- main elements of a formal proof from a decorated program. Indeed, the
488+-- process is so straightforward that it can be automated, as we will see
489+-- next.
490+
491+-- ## Formal Decorated Programs
492+
493+-- Our informal conventions for decorated programs amount to a way of
494+-- "displaying" Hoare triples, in which commands are annotated with enough
495+-- embedded assertions that checking the validity of a triple is reduced to
496+-- simple logical and algebraic calculations showing that some assertions
497+-- imply others.
498+
499+-- In this section, we show that this presentation style can be made
500+-- completely formal — and indeed that checking the validity of decorated
501+-- programs can be largely automated.
502+
503+-- ### Syntax
504+
505+-- The first thing we need to do is to formalize a variant of the syntax of
506+-- Imp commands that includes embedded assertions, which we'll call
507+-- "decorations." We call the new commands *decorated commands*, or `dcom`s.
508+
509+-- The choice of exactly where to put assertions in the definition of `dcom`
510+-- is a bit subtle. The simplest thing to do would be to annotate every `dcom`
511+-- with a precondition and postcondition — something like this...
512+
513+namespace DComFirstTry
514+
515+inductive DCom where
516+  | skip (pre : Assertion)
517+  | seq (pre : Assertion) (first : DCom)
518+      (middle : Assertion)
519+      (second : DCom) (post : Assertion)
520+  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (post : Assertion)
521+  | cond (pre : Assertion) (b : Bexp)
522+      (thenPre : Assertion) (thenBranch : DCom)
523+      (elsePre : Assertion) (elseBranch : DCom)
524+      (post : Assertion)
525+  | whileDo (pre : Assertion) (b : Bexp)
526+      (bodyPre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
527+      (bodyPost : Assertion) (post : Assertion)
528+  | strengthenPre (pre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
529+  | weakenPost (body : DCom) (post : Assertion)
530+
531+end DComFirstTry
532+
533+-- But this would result in *very* verbose decorated programs with a lot of
534+-- repeated annotations: a simple program like `skip;skip` would be decorated
535+-- like this,
536+
537+--   {{P}} ({{P}} skip {{P}}) ; ({{P}} skip {{P}}) {{P}}
538+
539+-- with pre- and post-conditions around each `skip`, plus identical pre- and
540+-- post-conditions on the semicolon!
541+
542+-- In other words, we don't want both preconditions and postconditions on each
543+-- command, because a sequence of two commands would contain redundant
544+-- decorations — the postcondition of the first likely being the same as the
545+-- precondition of the second.
546+
547+-- Instead, our formal syntax of decorated commands will omit preconditions
548+-- whenever possible and embed just postconditions.
549+
550+-- - The `skip` command, for example, is decorated only with its postcondition
551+
552+--   skip {{ Q }}
553+
554+-- on the assumption that the precondition will be provided by somebody else.
555+
556+-- We carry the same assumption through the other syntactic forms: each
557+-- decorated command is assumed to carry its own postcondition within itself
558+-- but take its precondition from its context in which it is used.
559+
560+-- - Sequences `d1 ; d2` need no additional decorations.
561+
562+-- Why?
563+
564+-- Because inside `d2` there will be a postcondition, which also serves as the
565+-- postcondition of `d1;d2`.
566+
567+-- Similarly, inside `d1` there will also be a postcondition, which
568+-- additionally serves as the *precondition* for `d2`.
569+
570+-- - An assignment `X := a` is decorated only with its postcondition:
571+
572+--   X := a {{ Q }}
573+
574+-- - A conditional `if b then d1 else d2` is decorated with a postcondition for
575+--   the entire statement, as well as preconditions for each branch:
576+
577+--   if b then {{ P1 }} d1 else {{ P2 }} d2 end {{ Q }}
578+
579+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2025):
580+--     Maybe we need a note here about why we don't just calculate P1 and P2
581+--     later, once we know the precondition of the whole loop. Indeed, we
582+--     could (and perhaps should, as discussed elsewhere), but we are doing
583+--     something simpler for the moment.
584+
585+-- - A loop `while b do d end` is decorated with its final postcondition plus a
586+--   precondition for the body:
587+
588+--   while b do {{ P }} d end {{ Q }}
589+
590+-- The postcondition embedded in `d` serves as the loop invariant.
591+
592+-- - Implications `->>` can be added as decorations either for a precondition...
593+
594+--   ->> {{ P }} d
595+
596+-- ...or for a postcondition:
597+
598+--   d ->> {{ Q }}
599+
600+-- The former is waiting for another precondition to be supplied by the
601+-- context; the latter relies on the postcondition already embedded in `d`.
602+
603+-- Putting this all together gives us the formal syntax of decorated commands:
604+
605+inductive DCom where
606+  | skip (post : Assertion)
607+  | seq (first second : DCom)
608+  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (post : Assertion)
609+  | cond (b : Bexp)
610+      (thenPre : Assertion) (thenBranch : DCom)
611+      (elsePre : Assertion) (elseBranch : DCom)
612+      (post : Assertion)
613+  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (bodyPre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
614+      (post : Assertion)
615+  | pre (pre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
616+  | post (body : DCom) (post : Assertion)
617+
618+-- Lean keeps decorated-command notation in its own syntax category, `dcom`,
619+-- so it can coexist with the ordinary Imp command syntax.
620+
621+-- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: decorated commands
622+
623+declare_syntax_cat dcom
624+
625+syntax:max "(" dcom ")" : dcom
626+syntax:max "skip" " {{" term "}}" : dcom
627+syntax:max ident " := " imp_aexp " {{" term "}}" : dcom
628+syntax:20 dcom:21 ";" ppLine dcom:20 : dcom
629+syntax:max "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "then" ppLine
630+  "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
631+  "else" ppLine "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
632+  "end" ppLine "{{" term "}}" : dcom
633+syntax:max "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "do" ppLine
634+  "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
635+  "end" ppLine "{{" term "}}" : dcom
636+syntax:5 "->>" " {{" term "}}" ppLine dcom:0 : dcom
637+syntax:5 dcom:6 ppLine "->>" " {{" term "}}" : dcom
638+
639+syntax:min "dcom" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine dcom
640+  ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
641+
642+macro_rules
643+  | `(dcom { ($body:dcom) }) =>
644+      `(dcom { $body })
645+  | `(dcom { skip {{ $q }} }) =>
646+      `(DCom.skip ({{ $q }}))
647+  | `(dcom { $x:ident := $a:imp_aexp {{ $q }} }) =>
648+      `(DCom.asgn $x (aexp { $a }) ({{ $q }}))
649+  | `(dcom { $d1:dcom; $d2:dcom }) =>
650+      `(DCom.seq (dcom { $d1 }) (dcom { $d2 }))
651+  | `(dcom {
652+        if ($b:imp_bexp) then
653+          {{ $p1 }}
654+          $d1:dcom
655+        else
656+          {{ $p2 }}
657+          $d2:dcom
658+        end
659+          {{ $q }}
660+      }) =>
661+      `(DCom.cond (bexp { $b })
662+        ({{ $p1 }}) (dcom { $d1 })
663+        ({{ $p2 }}) (dcom { $d2 })
664+        ({{ $q }}))
665+  | `(dcom {
666+        while ($b:imp_bexp) do
667+          {{ $p }}
668+          $body:dcom
669+        end
670+          {{ $q }}
671+      }) =>
672+      `(DCom.whileDo (bexp { $b }) ({{ $p }})
673+        (dcom { $body }) ({{ $q }}))
674+  | `(dcom { ->> {{ $p }} $body:dcom }) =>
675+      `(DCom.pre ({{ $p }}) (dcom { $body }))
676+  | `(dcom { $body:dcom ->> {{ $q }} }) =>
677+      `(DCom.post (dcom { $body }) ({{ $q }}))
678+
679+-- END DETAILS
680+
681+-- To provide the initial precondition that goes at the very top of a
682+-- decorated program, we introduce a new type `decorated`:
683+
684+structure Decorated where
685+  pre : Assertion
686+  body : DCom
687+
688+-- Note to developers:
689+--     HIDE: Add FOLD here
690+
691+example : DCom :=
692+  .skip {{ True }}
693+
694+example : DCom :=
695+  .whileDo (bexp {true}) {{ True }}
696+    (.skip {{ True }}) {{ True }}
697+
698+-- To inspect the fully elaborated term behind this notation, put
699+-- `set_option pp.all true in` before a `#check` or `#print` command.
700+
701+-- The formal definitions can use either constructors directly or the
702+-- decorated-command notation introduced above.
703+
704+-- Note to developers:
705+--     HIDE: Add /FOLD here
706+
707+-- An example `decorated` program that decrements `X` to `0`:
708+
709+def decWhile : Decorated where
710+  pre := ({{ True }})
711+  body := dcom {
712+    while (X ≠ 0) do
713+      {{ True ∧ ¬ X = 0 }}
714+      X := X - 1 {{ True }}
715+    end
716+      {{ True ∧ X = 0 }}
717+    ->> {{ X = 0 }}
718+  }
719+
720+-- It is easy to go from a `dcom` to a `com` by erasing all annotations.
721+
722+def DCom.erase (d : DCom) : Com :=
723+  match d with
724+  | .skip _ => .skip
725+  | .seq d1 d2 => .seq d1.erase d2.erase
726+  | .asgn x a _ => .asgn x a
727+  | .cond b _ d1 _ d2 _ => .cond b d1.erase d2.erase
728+  | .whileDo b _ body _ => .whileDo b body.erase
729+  | .pre _ body => body.erase
730+  | .post body _ => body.erase
731+
732+def Decorated.erase (dec : Decorated) : Com :=
733+  dec.body.erase
734+
735+example :
736+    decWhile.erase =
737+      (imp {
738+        while (X ≠ 0) {
739+          X := X - 1;
740+        }
741+      }) := by
742+  rfl
743+
744+-- It is also straightforward to extract the precondition and postcondition
745+-- from a decorated program.
746+
747+def Decorated.precondition (dec : Decorated) : Assertion :=
748+  dec.pre
749+
750+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2025):
751+--     `It would be nice to use <{ ... }> notations
752+--     in this definition and the ones below...
753+--          | <{ skip {{P}} }>        => P
754+--          | <{ _; d2 }>             => post d2
755+--          | <{ _ := _ {{Q}} }>      => Q`
756+
757+def DCom.postcondition (d : DCom) : Assertion :=
758+  match d with
759+  | .skip q => q
760+  | .seq _ d2 => d2.postcondition
761+  | .asgn _ _ q => q
762+  | .cond _ _ _ _ _ q => q
763+  | .whileDo _ _ _ q => q
764+  | .pre _ body => body.postcondition
765+  | .post _ q => q
766+
767+def Decorated.postcondition (dec : Decorated) : Assertion :=
768+  dec.body.postcondition
769+
770+example : decWhile.precondition = {{ True }} := by
771+  funext st
772+  rfl
773+
774+example : decWhile.postcondition = {{ X = 0 }} := by
775+  funext st
776+  rfl
777+
778+-- We can then express what it means for a decorated program to be correct as
779+-- follows:
780+
781+def Decorated.OuterTripleValid (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
782+  ValidHoareTriple dec.precondition dec.erase
783+    dec.postcondition
784+
785+-- For example:
786+
787+example :
788+    decWhile.OuterTripleValid =
789+      ValidHoareTriple
790+        {{ True }}
791+        (imp {
792+          while (X ≠ 0) {
793+            X := X - 1;
794+          }
795+        })
796+        {{ X = 0 }} := by
797+  rfl
798+
799+-- The outer Hoare triple of a decorated program is just a `Prop`; thus, to
800+-- show that it is *valid*, we need to produce a proof of this proposition.
801+
802+-- We will do this by extracting "proof obligations" from the decorations
803+-- sprinkled throughout the program.
804+
805+-- These obligations are often called *verification conditions*, because they
806+-- are the facts that must be verified to see that the decorations are locally
807+-- consistent and thus constitute a proof of validity of the outer triple.
808+
809+-- ### Extracting Verification Conditions
810+
811+-- The function `DCom.VerificationConditions` takes a decorated command `d`
812+-- together with a precondition `P` and returns a *proposition* that, if it
813+-- can be proved, implies that the triple
814+
815+--   {{P}} d.erase {{d.postcondition}}
816+
817+-- is valid.
818+
819+-- It does this by walking over `d` and generating a big conjunction that
820+-- includes
821+
822+-- - local consistency checks for each form of command, plus
823+
824+-- - uses of `->>` to bridge the gap between the assertions found inside a
825+--   decorated command and the assertions imposed by the external precondition;
826+--   these uses correspond to applications of the consequence rule.
827+
828+-- *Local consistency* is defined as follows...
829+
830+-- - The decorated command
831+
832+--   skip {{Q}}
833+
834+-- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if `P ->> Q`.
835+
836+-- - The sequential composition of `d1` and `d2` is locally consistent with
837+--   respect to `P` if `d1` is locally consistent with respect to `P` and `d2`
838+--   is locally consistent with respect to the postcondition of `d1`.
839+
840+-- - An assignment
841+
842+--   X := a {{Q}}
843+
844+-- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
845+
846+--   P ->> Q [X |-> a]
847+
848+-- - A conditional
849+
850+--   if b then {{P1}} d1 else {{P2}} d2 end {{Q}}
851+
852+-- is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P` if
853+
854+-- (1) `P /\ b ->> P1`
855+
856+-- (2) `P /\ ~b ->> P2`
857+
858+-- (3) `d1` is locally consistent with respect to `P1`
859+
860+-- (4) `d2` is locally consistent with respect to `P2`
861+
862+-- (5) `d1.postcondition ->> Q`
863+
864+-- (6) `d2.postcondition ->> Q`
865+
866+-- - A loop
867+
868+--   while b do {{Q}} d end {{R}}
869+
870+-- is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P` if:
871+
872+-- (1) `P ->> d.postcondition`
873+
874+-- (2) `d.postcondition /\ b ->> Q`
875+
876+-- (3) `d.postcondition /\ ~b ->> R`
877+
878+-- (4) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
879+
880+-- - A command with an extra assertion at the beginning
881+
882+--   ->> {{Q}} d
883+
884+-- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
885+
886+-- (1) `P ->> Q`
887+
888+-- (2) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
889+
890+-- - A command with an extra assertion at the end
891+
892+--   d ->> {{Q}}
893+
894+-- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
895+
896+-- (1) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `P`
897+
898+-- (2) `d.postcondition ->> Q`
899+
900+-- With all this in mind, we can write a *verification condition generator*
901+-- that takes a decorated command and reads off a proposition saying that all
902+-- its decorations are locally consistent.
903+
904+-- Formally, since a decorated command is "waiting for its precondition" the
905+-- main VC generator takes a `dcom` plus a given precondition as arguments.
906+
907+-- Note to developers:
908+--     HIDE: There was some discussion in 2016 about whether the VC generator
909+--     should should use equivalence or implication in a few places. I (BCP)
910+--     believe Phil (Wadler) changed some instances of the former to the
911+--     latter.
912+--
913+--     HIDE: MRC'20: a written explanation of each part of this would be quite
914+--     nice. BCP 21: Agreed!! (BCP 23: But it's kind of what's just above...)
915+
916+def DCom.VerificationConditions
917+    (P : Assertion) (d : DCom) : Prop :=
918+  match d with
919+  | .skip Q =>
920+      P ->> Q
921+  | .seq d1 d2 =>
922+      d1.VerificationConditions P ∧
923+      d2.VerificationConditions d1.postcondition
924+  | .asgn x a Q =>
925+      P ->> Q [x ↦ ~a]
926+  | .cond b P1 d1 P2 d2 Q =>
927+      ({{ P ∧ b }} ->> P1) ∧
928+      ({{ P ∧ ¬ b }} ->> P2) ∧
929+      (d1.postcondition ->> Q) ∧
930+      (d2.postcondition ->> Q) ∧
931+      d1.VerificationConditions P1 ∧
932+      d2.VerificationConditions P2
933+  | .whileDo b bodyPre body q =>
934+      -- The body's postcondition is both the loop invariant
935+      -- and the precondition for the first iteration.
936+      (P ->> body.postcondition) ∧
937+      ({{ body.postcondition ∧ b }} ->> bodyPre) ∧
938+      ({{ body.postcondition ∧ ¬ b }} ->> q) ∧
939+      body.VerificationConditions bodyPre
940+  | .pre P' body =>
941+      (P ->> P') ∧ body.VerificationConditions P'
942+  | .post body Q =>
943+      body.VerificationConditions P ∧
944+      (body.postcondition ->> Q)
945+
946+-- The following key theorem states that `DCom.VerificationConditions` does
947+-- its job correctly. Not surprisingly, each of the Hoare Logic rules plays a
948+-- critical role at some point in the proof.
949+
950+theorem verification_correct (d : DCom) (P : Assertion)
951+    (hvc : d.VerificationConditions P) :
952+    ValidHoareTriple P d.erase d.postcondition := by
953+  sorry
954+
955+-- Now that all the pieces are in place, we can define what it means to verify
956+-- an entire program.
957+
958+def Decorated.VerificationConditions
959+    (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
960+  dec.body.VerificationConditions dec.pre
961+
962+-- And this brings us to the main theorem of this section:
963+
964+theorem verification_conditions_correct (dec : Decorated)
965+    (hvc : dec.VerificationConditions) :
966+    dec.OuterTripleValid := by
967+  exact verification_correct dec.body dec.pre hvc
968+
969+-- ### More Automation
970+
971+-- The propositions generated by `DCom.VerificationConditions` are fairly big
972+-- and contain many conjuncts that are essentially trivial.
973+
974+-- Note to developers:
975+--     `HIDE: MRC'20: The conditions here used to be just [Eval]ed instead
976+--     of being duplicated in a comment.  They were actually incorrect
977+--     because of changes to notation.  Putting them in as an [Example]
978+--     will force us to keep them up-to-date. APT20: Yes, but but stating
979+--     this an equality completely misses the point about verify_assertion! So I
980+--     changed things back.`
981+
982+example : decWhile.VerificationConditions := by
983+  unfold Decorated.VerificationConditions decWhile
984+  simp only [DCom.VerificationConditions,
985+    DCom.postcondition]
986+  sorry
987+
988+-- Fortunately, our `verify_assertion` tactic can generally take care of most
989+-- (or sometimes all) of them.
990+
991+example : decWhile.VerificationConditions := by
992+  sorry
993+
994+-- To automate the overall process of verification, we can use
995+-- `verification_correct` to extract the verification conditions, use
996+-- `verify_assertion` to verify them as much as it can, and finally tidy up
997+-- any remaining bits by hand.
998+
999+macro "verify" : tactic =>
1000+  `(tactic|
1001+    (apply verification_conditions_correct;
1002+     verify_assertion))
1003+
1004+-- Here's the final, formal proof that `decWhile` is correct.
1005+
1006+theorem dec_while_correct :
1007+    decWhile.OuterTripleValid := by
1008+  sorry
1009+
1010+-- Similarly, here is the formal decorated program for the "swapping by adding
1011+-- and subtracting" example that we saw earlier.
1012+
1013+def swapDec (m n : Nat) : Decorated where
1014+  pre := ({{ X = m ∧ Y = n }})
1015+  body := dcom {
1016+    ->> {{ (X + Y) - ((X + Y) - Y) = n ∧ (X + Y) - Y = m }}
1017+    X := X + Y {{ X - (X - Y) = n ∧ X - Y = m }};
1018+    Y := X - Y {{ X - Y = n ∧ Y = m }};
1019+    X := X - Y {{ X = n ∧ Y = m }}
1020+  }
1021+
1022+theorem swap_correct (m n : Nat) :
1023+    (swapDec m n).OuterTripleValid := by
1024+  sorry
1025+
1026+-- And here is the formal decorated version of the "positive difference"
1027+-- program from earlier:
1028+
1029+def positiveDifferenceDec : Decorated where
1030+  pre := ({{ True }})
1031+  body := dcom {
1032+    if (X ≤ Y) then
1033+      {{ True ∧ X ≤ Y }}
1034+      ->> {{ (Y - X) + X = Y ∨ (Y - X) + Y = X }}
1035+      Z := Y - X {{ Z + X = Y ∨ Z + Y = X }}
1036+    else
1037+      {{ True ∧ ¬ X ≤ Y }}
1038+      ->> {{ (X - Y) + X = Y ∨ (X - Y) + Y = X }}
1039+      Z := X - Y {{ Z + X = Y ∨ Z + Y = X }}
1040+    end
1041+      {{ Z + X = Y ∨ Z + Y = X }}
1042+  }
1043+
1044+theorem positive_difference_correct :
1045+    positiveDifferenceDec.OuterTripleValid := by
1046+  sorry
1047+
1048+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): if_minus_plus_correct ⭐⭐
1049+
1050+-- Here is a skeleton of the formal decorated version of the `if_minus_plus`
1051+-- program that we saw earlier. Replace all occurrences of `FILL_IN_HERE` with
1052+-- appropriate assertions and fill in the proof (which should be just as
1053+-- straightforward as in the examples above).
1054+
1055+def ifMinusPlusDec : Decorated where
1056+  pre := ({{ True }})
1057+  body := dcom {
1058+    if (X ≤ Y) then
1059+      {{ True ∧ X ≤ Y }}
1060+      ->> {{ Y = X + (Y - X) }}
1061+      Z := Y - X {{ Y = X + Z }}
1062+    else
1063+      {{ True ∧ ¬ X ≤ Y }}
1064+      ->> {{ X + Z = X + Z }}
1065+      Y := X + Z {{ Y = X + Z }}
1066+    end
1067+      {{ Y = X + Z }}
1068+  }
1069+
1070+theorem if_minus_plus_correct :
1071+    ifMinusPlusDec.OuterTripleValid := by
1072+  all_goals
1073+    sorry
1074+
1075+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): div_mod_outer_triple_valid ⭐⭐
1076+
1077+-- Fill in appropriate assertions for the division program from above.
1078+
1079+def divModDec (a b : Nat) : Decorated where
1080+  pre := ({{ True }})
1081+  body := dcom {
1082+    ->> {{ b * 0 + a = a }}
1083+    X := ~(Aexp.num a) {{ b * 0 + X = a }};
1084+    Y := 0 {{ b * Y + X = a }};
1085+    while (~(Aexp.num b) ≤ X) do
1086+      {{ b * Y + X = a ∧ b ≤ X }}
1087+      ->> {{ b * (Y + 1) + (X - b) = a }}
1088+      X := X - ~(Aexp.num b) {{ b * (Y + 1) + X = a }};
1089+      Y := Y + 1 {{ b * Y + X = a }}
1090+    end
1091+      {{ b * Y + X = a ∧ ¬ b ≤ X }}
1092+    ->> {{ b * Y + X = a ∧ X < b }}
1093+  }
1094+
1095+theorem div_mod_outer_triple_valid (a b : Nat) :
1096+    (divModDec a b).OuterTripleValid := by
1097+  all_goals
1098+    sorry
1099+
1100+-- ## Finding Loop Invariants
1101+
1102+-- Once the outermost precondition and postcondition are chosen, the only
1103+-- creative part of a verifying program using Hoare Logic is finding the right
1104+-- loop invariants. The reason this is difficult is the same as the reason
1105+-- that inductive mathematical proofs are:
1106+
1107+-- - Strengthening a *loop invariant* means that you have a stronger assumption
1108+--   to work with when trying to establish the postcondition of the loop body,
1109+--   but it also means that the loop body's postcondition is harder to prove.
1110+
1111+-- - Similarly, strengthening an *induction hypothesis* means that you have a
1112+--   stronger assumption to work with when trying to complete the induction step
1113+--   of the proof, but it also means that the statement being proved inductively
1114+--   is harder to prove.
1115+
1116+-- This section explains how to approach the challenge of finding loop
1117+-- invariants through a series of examples and exercises.
1118+
1119+-- ### Example: Slow Subtraction
1120+
1121+-- The following program subtracts the value of `X` from the value of `Y` by
1122+-- repeatedly decrementing both `X` and `Y`. We want to verify its correctness
1123+-- with respect to the pre- and postconditions shown:
1124+
1125+--   {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}
1126+--     while X <> 0 do
1127+--       Y := Y - 1;
1128+--       X := X - 1
1129+--     end
1130+--   {{ Y = n - m }}
1131+
1132+-- To verify this program, we need to find an invariant `Inv` for the loop. As
1133+-- a first step we can leave `Inv` as an unknown and build a *skeleton* for
1134+-- the proof by applying the rules for local consistency, working from the end
1135+-- of the program to the beginning, as usual, and without doing any thinking
1136+-- at all yet.
1137+
1138+-- This leads to the following skeleton:
1139+
1140+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}  ->>                   (a)
1141+--   (2)    {{ Inv }}
1142+--            while X <> 0 do
1143+--   (3)              {{ Inv /\ X <> 0 }}  ->>          (c)
1144+--   (4)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] [Y |-> Y-1] }}
1145+--              Y := Y - 1;
1146+--   (5)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] }}
1147+--              X := X - 1
1148+--   (6)              {{ Inv }}
1149+--            end
1150+--   (7)    {{ Inv /\ ~ (X <> 0) }}  ->>                (b)
1151+--   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1152+
1153+-- Examining this skeleton, we can see that any valid `Inv` will have to
1154+-- respect three conditions:
1155+
1156+-- - (a) it must be *weak* enough to be implied by the loop's precondition,
1157+--   i.e., (1) must imply (2);
1158+
1159+-- - (b) it must be *strong* enough to imply the program's postcondition, i.e.,
1160+--   (7) must imply (8);
1161+
1162+-- - (c) it must be *preserved* by a single iteration of the loop, assuming that
1163+--   the loop guard also evaluates to true, i.e., (3) must imply (4).
1164+
1165+-- These conditions are actually independent of the particular program and
1166+-- specification we are considering: every loop invariant has to satisfy them.
1167+
1168+-- One way to find a loop invariant that simultaneously satisfies these three
1169+-- conditions is by using an iterative process: start with a "candidate"
1170+-- invariant (e.g., a guess or a heuristic choice) and check the three
1171+-- conditions above; if any of the checks fails, try to use the information
1172+-- that we get from the failure to produce another — hopefully better —
1173+-- candidate invariant, and repeat.
1174+
1175+-- For instance, in the reduce-to-zero example above, we saw that, for a very
1176+-- simple loop, choosing `True` as a loop invariant did the job. Maybe it will
1177+-- work here too. To find out, let's try instantiating `Inv` with `True` in
1178+-- the skeleton above and see what we get...
1179+
1180+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                    (a - OK)
1181+--   (2)    {{ True }}
1182+--            while X <> 0 do
1183+--   (3)                   {{ True /\ X <> 0 }} ->>     (c - OK)
1184+--   (4)                   {{ True }}
1185+--              Y := Y - 1;
1186+--   (5)                   {{ True }}
1187+--              X := X - 1
1188+--   (6)                   {{ True }}
1189+--            end
1190+--   (7)    {{ True /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                 (b - WRONG!)
1191+--   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1192+
1193+-- While conditions (a) and (c) are trivially satisfied, (b) is wrong: it is
1194+-- not the case that `True /\ X = 0` (7) implies `Y = n - m` (8). In fact, the
1195+-- two assertions are completely unrelated, so it is very easy to find a
1196+-- counterexample to the implication (say, `Y = X = m = 0` and `n = 1`).
1197+
1198+-- If we want (b) to hold, we need to strengthen the loop invariant so that it
1199+-- implies the postcondition (8). One simple way to do this is to let the loop
1200+-- invariant *be* the postcondition. So let's return to our skeleton,
1201+-- instantiate `Inv` with `Y = n - m`, and try checking conditions (a) to (c)
1202+-- again.
1203+
1204+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                        (a - WRONG!)
1205+--   (2)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1206+--            while X <> 0 do
1207+--   (3)                     {{ Y = n - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>  (c - WRONG!)
1208+--   (4)                     {{ Y - 1 = n - m }}
1209+--              Y := Y - 1;
1210+--   (5)                     {{ Y = n - m }}
1211+--              X := X - 1
1212+--   (6)                     {{ Y = n - m }}
1213+--            end
1214+--   (7)    {{ Y = n - m /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1215+--   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1216+
1217+-- This time, condition (b) holds trivially, but (a) and (c) are broken.
1218+-- Condition (a) requires that (1) `X = m /\ Y = n` implies (2) `Y = n - m`.
1219+-- If we substitute `Y` by `n` we have to show that `n = n - m` for arbitrary
1220+-- `m` and `n`, which is not the case (for instance, when `m = n = 1`).
1221+-- Condition (c) requires that `n - m - 1 = n - m`, which fails, for instance,
1222+-- for `n = 1` and `m = 0`. So, although `Y = n - m` holds at the end of the
1223+-- loop, it does not hold from the start, and it doesn't hold on each
1224+-- iteration; it is not a correct loop invariant.
1225+
1226+-- This failure is not very surprising: the variable `Y` changes during the
1227+-- loop, while `m` and `n` are constant, so the assertion we chose didn't have
1228+-- much chance of being a loop invariant!
1229+
1230+-- To do better, we need to generalize (7) to some statement that is
1231+-- equivalent to (8) when `X` is `0`, since this will be the case when the
1232+-- loop terminates, and that "fills the gap" in some appropriate way when `X`
1233+-- is nonzero. Looking at how the loop works, we can observe that `X` and `Y`
1234+-- are decremented together until `X` reaches `0`. So, if `X = 2` and `Y = 5`
1235+-- initially, after one iteration of the loop we obtain `X = 1` and `Y = 4`;
1236+-- after two iterations `X = 0` and `Y = 3`; and then the loop stops. Notice
1237+-- that the difference between `Y` and `X` stays constant between iterations:
1238+-- initially, `Y = n` and `X = m`, and the difference is always `n - m`. So
1239+-- let's try instantiating `Inv` in the skeleton above with `Y - X = n - m`.
1240+
1241+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                            (a - OK)
1242+--   (2)    {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1243+--            while X <> 0 do
1244+--   (3)                    {{ Y - X = n - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>   (c - OK)
1245+--   (4)                    {{ (Y - 1) - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1246+--              Y := Y - 1;
1247+--   (5)                    {{ Y - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1248+--              X := X - 1
1249+--   (6)                    {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1250+--            end
1251+--   (7)    {{ Y - X = n - m /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1252+--   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1253+
1254+-- Success! Conditions (a), (b) and (c) all hold now. (To verify (c), we need
1255+-- to check that, under the assumption that `X <> 0`, we have
1256+-- `Y - X = (Y - 1) - (X - 1)`; this holds for all natural numbers `X` and
1257+-- `Y`.)
1258+
1259+-- Here is the final version of the decorated program:
1260+
1261+def subtractSlowlyDec (m n : Nat) : Decorated where
1262+  pre := ({{ X = m ∧ Y = n }})
1263+  body := dcom {
1264+    ->> {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1265+    while (X ≠ 0) do
1266+      {{ Y - X = n - m ∧ ¬ X = 0 }}
1267+      ->> {{ (Y - 1) - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1268+      Y := Y - 1 {{ Y - (X - 1) = n - m }};
1269+      X := X - 1 {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1270+    end
1271+      {{ Y - X = n - m ∧ X = 0 }}
1272+    ->> {{ Y = n - m }}
1273+  }
1274+
1275+theorem subtract_slowly_outer_triple_valid (m n : Nat) :
1276+    (subtractSlowlyDec m n).OuterTripleValid := by
1277+  sorry
1278+
1279+-- ### Exercise: Slow Assignment
1280+
1281+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): slow_assignment ⭐⭐
1282+
1283+-- A roundabout way of assigning a number currently stored in `X` to the
1284+-- variable `Y` is to start `Y` at `0`, then decrement `X` until it hits `0`,
1285+-- incrementing `Y` at each step. Here is a program that implements this idea.
1286+-- Fill in decorations and prove the decorated program correct. (The proof
1287+-- should be very simple.)
1288+
1289+def slowAssignmentDec (m : Nat) : Decorated where
1290+  pre := ({{ X = m }})
1291+  body := dcom {
1292+    Y := 0 {{ ({{ X = m ∧ Y = 0 }}) }};
1293+    (->> {{ ({{ Y + X = m }}) }}
1294+      while (X ≠ 0) do
1295+        {{ ({{ Y + X = m ∧ ¬ X = 0 }}) }}
1296+        ->> {{ ({{ Y + (X - 1) + 1 = m }}) }}
1297+        X := X - 1 {{ ({{ Y + X + 1 = m }}) }};
1298+        (->> {{ ({{ Y + X + 1 = m }}) }}
1299+          Y := Y + 1 {{ ({{ Y + X = m }}) }})
1300+      end
1301+        {{ ({{ Y + X = m ∧ X = 0 }}) }}
1302+      ->> {{ Y = m }})
1303+  }
1304+
1305+theorem slow_assignment (m : Nat) :
1306+    (slowAssignmentDec m).OuterTripleValid := by
1307+  all_goals
1308+    sorry
1309+
1310+-- ### Example: Parity
1311+
1312+-- Here is a cute way of computing the parity of a value initially stored in
1313+-- `X`, due to Daniel Cristofani.
1314+
1315+--   {{ X = m }}
1316+--     while 2 <= X do
1317+--       X := X - 2
1318+--     end
1319+--   {{ X = parity m }}
1320+
1321+-- The `parity` function used in the specification is defined in Lean as
1322+-- follows:
1323+
1324+def parity : Nat → Nat
1325+  | 0 => 0
1326+  | 1 => 1
1327+  | Nat.succ (Nat.succ n) => parity n
1328+
1329+-- The postcondition does not hold at the beginning of the loop, since
1330+-- `m = parity m` does not hold for an arbitrary `m`, so we cannot hope to use
1331+-- that as a loop invariant. To find a loop invariant that works, let's think
1332+-- a bit about what this loop does. On each iteration it decrements `X` by
1333+-- `2`, which preserves the parity of `X`. So the parity of `X` does not
1334+-- change, i.e., it is invariant. The initial value of `X` is `m`, so the
1335+-- parity of `X` is always equal to the parity of `m`. Using
1336+-- `parity X = parity m` as an invariant we obtain the following decorated
1337+-- program:
1338+
1339+--   {{ X = m }} ->>                                         (a - OK)
1340+--   {{ parity X = parity m }}
1341+--     while 2 <= X do
1342+--                  {{ parity X = parity m /\ 2 <= X }} ->>  (c - OK)
1343+--                  {{ parity (X-2) = parity m }}
1344+--       X := X - 2
1345+--                  {{ parity X = parity m }}
1346+--     end
1347+--   {{ parity X = parity m /\ ~(2 <= X) }} ->>              (b - OK)
1348+--   {{ X = parity m }}
1349+
1350+-- With this loop invariant, conditions (a), (b), and (c) are all satisfied.
1351+-- For verifying (b), we observe that, when `X < 2`, we have `parity X = X`
1352+-- (we can easily see this in the definition of `parity`). For verifying (c),
1353+-- we observe that, when `2 <= X`, we have `parity X = parity (X-2)`.
1354+
1355+-- Note to developers:
1356+--     `HIDE: A more complexly phrased loop invariant for the same program
1357+--     [[
1358+--             {{ X = m }}  ->>                        (a - OK)
1359+--             {{ ev X <-> ev m }}
1360+--           while 2 <= X do
1361+--               {{ ev X <-> ev m /\ 2 <= X }}  ->>    (c - OK)
1362+--               {{ ev (X-2) <-> ev m }}
1363+--             X := X - 2
1364+--               {{ ev X <-> ev m }}
1365+--           end
1366+--             {{ (ev X <-> ev m) /\ ~(2 <= X) }}  ->>     (b - OK)
1367+--             {{ X=0 <-> ev m }}
1368+--     ]]`
1369+--
1370+--     `HIDE: find_parity'_dec; more complicated phrasing of invariant
1371+--     there is very little resemblance between the invariant and the
1372+--     postcondition -- the implication is also non-obvious, and the
1373+--     X <= m condition makes the invariant more complicated
1374+--     [[
1375+--      {{ X = m }} ->>
1376+--      {{ X <= m /\ ev (m - X) }}
1377+--     while 2 <= X do
1378+--        {{ X <= m /\ ev (m - X) /\ 2 <= X }} ->>
1379+--        {{ X - 2 <= m /\ ev (m - (X - 2)) }}
1380+--      X := X - 2
1381+--        {{ X <= m /\ ev (m - X) }}
1382+--     end
1383+--      {{ X <= m /\ ev (m - X) /\ ~(2 <= X) }} ->>
1384+--      {{ X=0 <-> ev m }}
1385+--     ]]`
1386+
1387+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): parity ⭐⭐⭐
1388+
1389+-- Translate the above informal decorated program into a formal one and prove
1390+-- it correct.
1391+
1392+-- Hint: There are actually several possible loop invariants that all lead to
1393+-- good proofs; one that leads to a particularly simple proof is
1394+-- `parity X = parity m`. Ordinary Lean functions can be applied directly to
1395+-- Imp variables inside assertions, so this can be written as
1396+-- `{{ parity X = parity m }}`.
1397+
1398+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2023):
1399+--     `Maya: In the parity exercise, I was getting annoyed
1400+--     by the verify_assertion tactic unfolding the assumption [(2 <=?  st
1401+--     X) = true] into a match on the first two layers of [st X]. I ended
1402+--     up digging out the following incantation from the depths of the Rocq
1403+--     manual:
1404+--
1405+--        Arguments leb !n !m.
1406+--
1407+--     I'm not sure what level of automated tests you keep for the
1408+--     exercises, so I wanted to point this struggle out. Perhaps
1409+--     something changed in the Rocq library at some point.
1410+--
1411+--     BCP 23: Worth looking into!  (I tried just adding [Arguments leb !n
1412+--     !m.] to the script, but that broke things.)`
1413+
1414+def parityDec (m : Nat) : Decorated where
1415+  pre := ({{ X = m }})
1416+  body :=
1417+    let inv : Assertion :=
1418+      (fun st => parity (st X) = parity m)
1419+    let guardedInv : Assertion :=
1420+      (fun st =>
1421+        parity (st X) = parity m ∧ 2 ≤ st X)
1422+    let bodyPre : Assertion :=
1423+      (fun st => parity (st X - 2) = parity m)
1424+    let exit : Assertion :=
1425+      (fun st =>
1426+        parity (st X) = parity m ∧ ¬ 2 ≤ st X)
1427+    let post : Assertion :=
1428+      fun st => st X = parity m
1429+    dcom {
1430+    ->> {{ inv }}
1431+    while (2 ≤ X) do
1432+      {{ guardedInv }}
1433+      ->> {{ bodyPre }}
1434+      X := X - 2 {{ inv }}
1435+    end
1436+      {{ exit }}
1437+    ->> {{ post }}
1438+  }
1439+
1440+-- If you use the suggested loop invariant, you may find the following two
1441+-- lemmas helpful.
1442+
1443+theorem parity_ge_2 (x : Nat) (h : 2 ≤ x) :
1444+    parity (x - 2) = parity x := by
1445+  sorry
1446+
1447+theorem parity_lt_2 (x : Nat) (h : ¬ 2 ≤ x) :
1448+    parity x = x := by
1449+  sorry
1450+
1451+theorem parity_outer_triple_valid (m : Nat) :
1452+    (parityDec m).OuterTripleValid := by
1453+  all_goals
1454+    -- Simplification is too aggressive here; recover the
1455+    -- folded guard before proving preservation and exit.
1456+    sorry
1457+
1458+/- Here is another loop invariant — arguably a more natural
1459+one —
1460+which sadly leads to a rather long proof. -/
1461+inductive Even : Nat → Prop where
1462+  | zero : Even 0
1463+  | addTwo {n : Nat} : Even n → Even (Nat.succ (Nat.succ n))
1464+
1465+def findParityDec (m : Nat) : Decorated where
1466+  pre := ({{ X = m }})
1467+  body :=
1468+    let inv : Assertion :=
1469+      fun st => st X ≤ m ∧ Even (m - st X)
1470+    let guardedInv : Assertion :=
1471+      fun st => (st X ≤ m ∧ Even (m - st X)) ∧ 2 ≤ st X
1472+    let bodyPre : Assertion :=
1473+      fun st => st X - 2 ≤ m ∧ Even (m - (st X - 2))
1474+    let exit : Assertion :=
1475+      fun st => (st X ≤ m ∧ Even (m - st X)) ∧ st X < 2
1476+    let post : Assertion := fun st => st X = 0 ↔ Even m
1477+    dcom {
1478+    ->> {{ inv }}
1479+    while (2 ≤ X) do
1480+      {{ guardedInv }}
1481+      ->> {{ bodyPre }}
1482+      X := X - 2 {{ inv }}
1483+    end
1484+      {{ exit }}
1485+    ->> {{ post }}
1486+  }
1487+
1488+theorem find_parity_correct (m : Nat) :
1489+    (findParityDec m).OuterTripleValid := by
1490+  -- Simplification is too aggressive here; recover the
1491+  -- folded guard before proving preservation and exit.
1492+  -- At loop exit, X can only be 0 or 1.
1493+  sorry
1494+
1495+/- Here is a more intuitive way of writing the loop
1496+invariant. -/
1497+def findParityDec' (m : Nat) : Decorated where
1498+  pre := ({{ X = m }})
1499+  body :=
1500+    let inv : Assertion := fun st => Even (st X) ↔ Even m
1501+    let guardedInv : Assertion :=
1502+      fun st => (Even (st X) ↔ Even m) ∧ 2 ≤ st X
1503+    let bodyPre : Assertion :=
1504+      fun st => Even (st X - 2) ↔ Even m
1505+    let exit : Assertion :=
1506+      fun st => (Even (st X) ↔ Even m) ∧ ¬ 2 ≤ st X
1507+    let post : Assertion := fun st => st X = 0 ↔ Even m
1508+    dcom {
1509+    ->> {{ inv }}
1510+    while (2 ≤ X) do
1511+      {{ guardedInv }}
1512+      ->> {{ bodyPre }}
1513+      X := X - 2 {{ inv }}
1514+    end
1515+      {{ exit }}
1516+    ->> {{ post }}
1517+  }
1518+
1519+theorem find_parity_correct' (m : Nat) :
1520+    (findParityDec' m).OuterTripleValid := by
1521+  -- Simplification is too aggressive here; recover the
1522+  -- folded guard before proving preservation and exit.
1523+  -- At loop exit, X can only be 0 or 1.
1524+  sorry
1525+
1526+/- Finally, just for fun, here is an old-style
1527+non-decorated-program proof. -/
1528+theorem parity_correct (m : Nat) :
1529+    ValidHoareTriple ({{ X = m }})
1530+      (imp {
1531+        while (2 ≤ X) {
1532+          X := X - 2;
1533+        }
1534+      })
1535+      (fun st => st X = parity m) := by
1536+  sorry
1537+
1538+-- ### Example: Finding Square Roots
1539+
1540+-- The following program computes the integer square root of `X` by naive
1541+-- iteration:
1542+
1543+--   {{ X=m }}
1544+--     Z := 0;
1545+--     while (Z+1)*(Z+1) <= X do
1546+--       Z := Z+1
1547+--     end
1548+--   {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }}
1549+
1550+-- WORK IN CLASS
1551+
1552+-- As we did before, we can try to use the postcondition as a candidate loop
1553+-- invariant, obtaining the following decorated program:
1554+
1555+--   (1)  {{ X=m }} ->>                  (a - second conjunct of (2) WRONG!)
1556+--   (2)  {{ 0*0 <= m /\ m<(0+1)*(0+1) }}
1557+--           Z := 0
1558+--   (3)            {{ Z*Z <= m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }};
1559+--           while (Z+1)*(Z+1) <= X do
1560+--   (4)            {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1)
1561+--                            /\ (Z+1)*(Z+1)<=X }} ->>          (c - WRONG!)
1562+--   (5)            {{ (Z+1)*(Z+1)<=m /\ m<((Z+1)+1)*((Z+1)+1) }}
1563+--             Z := Z+1
1564+--   (6)            {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }}
1565+--           end
1566+--   (7)  {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) /\ ~((Z+1)*(Z+1)<=X) }} ->>    (b - OK)
1567+--   (8)  {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }}
1568+
1569+-- This didn't work very well: conditions (a) and (c) both failed. Looking at
1570+-- condition (c), we see that the second conjunct of (4) is almost the same as
1571+-- the first conjunct of (5), except that (4) mentions `X` while (5) mentions
1572+-- `m`. But note that `X` is never assigned in this program, so we should
1573+-- always have `X=m`. We didn't propagate this information from (1) into the
1574+-- loop invariant, but we could!
1575+
1576+-- Also, we don't need the second conjunct of (8), since we can obtain it from
1577+-- the negation of the guard — the third conjunct in (7) — again under the
1578+-- assumption that `X=m`. This allows us to simplify a bit.
1579+
1580+-- So we now try `X=m /\ Z*Z <= m` as the loop invariant:
1581+
1582+--   {{ X=m }} ->>                                           (a - OK)
1583+--   {{ X=m /\ 0*0 <= m }}
1584+--     Z := 0
1585+--                {{ X=m /\ Z*Z <= m }};
1586+--     while (Z+1)*(Z+1) <= X do
1587+--                {{ X=m /\ Z*Z<=m /\ (Z+1)*(Z+1)<=X }} ->>  (c - OK)
1588+--                {{ X=m /\ (Z+1)*(Z+1)<=m }}
1589+--       Z := Z + 1
1590+--                {{ X=m /\ Z*Z<=m }}
1591+--     end
1592+--   {{ X=m /\ Z*Z<=m /\ ~((Z+1)*(Z+1)<=X) }} ->>            (b - OK)
1593+--   {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }}
1594+
1595+-- This works, since conditions (a), (b), and (c) are now all rather trivially
1596+-- satisfied.
1597+
1598+-- Very often, when a variable is used in a loop in a read-only fashion (i.e.,
1599+-- it is referred to by the program or by the specification, and it is not
1600+-- changed by the loop), it is necessary to record the *fact* that it doesn't
1601+-- change in the loop invariant.
1602+
1603+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): sqrt ⭐⭐⭐
1604+
1605+-- Translate the above informal decorated program into a formal one and prove
1606+-- it correct.
1607+
1608+-- Hint: The loop invariant here must ensure that `Z*Z` is consistently less
1609+-- than or equal to X.
1610+
1611+def sqrtDec (m : Nat) : Decorated where
1612+  pre := ({{ X = m }})
1613+  body := dcom {
1614+    ->> {{ ({{ X = m ∧ 0 * 0 ≤ m }}) }}
1615+    Z := 0 {{ ({{ X = m ∧ Z * Z ≤ m }}) }};
1616+    while ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ X) do
1617+      {{ ({{
1618+        (X = m ∧ Z * Z ≤ m) ∧
1619+        (Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ X
1620+      }}) }}
1621+      ->> {{ ({{
1622+        X = m ∧ (Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m
1623+      }}) }}
1624+      Z := Z + 1 {{ ({{ X = m ∧ Z * Z ≤ m }}) }}
1625+    end
1626+      {{ ({{
1627+        (X = m ∧ Z * Z ≤ m) ∧
1628+        ¬ (Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ X
1629+      }}) }}
1630+    ->> {{ Z * Z ≤ m ∧ m < (Z + 1) * (Z + 1) }}
1631+  }
1632+
1633+theorem sqrt_correct (m : Nat) :
1634+    (sqrtDec m).OuterTripleValid := by
1635+  all_goals
1636+    sorry
1637+
1638+-- ### Example: Squaring
1639+
1640+-- Note to developers:
1641+--     HIDE: CH: it might make sense to show all the variants for future
1642+--     exercise builders, together with some hints on how to write programs
1643+--     that are easier to verify
1644+
1645+-- Here is a program that squares `X` by repeated addition:
1646+
1647+--   {{ X = m }}
1648+--     Y := 0;
1649+--     Z := 0;
1650+--     while Y <> X  do
1651+--       Z := Z + X;
1652+--       Y := Y + 1
1653+--     end
1654+--   {{ Z = m*m }}
1655+
1656+-- WORK IN CLASS
1657+
1658+-- The first thing to note is that the loop reads `X` but doesn't change its
1659+-- value. As we saw in the previous example, it can be a good idea in such
1660+-- cases to add `X = m` to the loop invariant. The other thing that we know is
1661+-- often useful in the loop invariant is the postcondition, so let's add that
1662+-- too, leading to the candidate loop invariant `Z = m * m /\ X = m`.
1663+
1664+--   {{ X = m }} ->>                                       (a - WRONG)
1665+--   {{ 0 = m*m /\ X = m }}
1666+--     Y := 0
1667+--                  {{ 0 = m*m /\ X = m }};
1668+--     Z := 0
1669+--                  {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m }};
1670+--     while Y <> X do
1671+--                  {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m /\ Y <> X }} ->>   (c - WRONG)
1672+--                  {{ Z+X = m*m /\ X = m }}
1673+--       Z := Z + X
1674+--                  {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m }};
1675+--       Y := Y + 1
1676+--                  {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m }}
1677+--     end
1678+--   {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m /\ ~(Y <> X) }} ->>               (b - OK)
1679+--   {{ Z = m*m }}
1680+
1681+-- Conditions (a) and (c) fail because of the `Z = m*m` part. While `Z` starts
1682+-- at `0` and works itself up to `m*m`, we can't expect `Z` to be `m*m` from
1683+-- the start. If we look at how `Z` progresses in the loop, after the 1st
1684+-- iteration `Z = m`, after the 2nd iteration `Z = 2*m`, and at the end
1685+-- `Z = m*m`. Since the variable `Y` tracks how many times we go through the
1686+-- loop, this leads us to derive a new loop invariant candidate:
1687+-- `Z = Y*m /\ X = m`.
1688+
1689+--   {{ X = m }} ->>                                        (a - OK)
1690+--   {{ 0 = 0*m /\ X = m }}
1691+--     Y := 0
1692+--                   {{ 0 = Y*m /\ X = m }};
1693+--     Z := 0
1694+--                   {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m }};
1695+--     while Y <> X do
1696+--                   {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m /\ Y <> X }} ->>   (c - OK)
1697+--                   {{ Z+X = (Y+1)*m /\ X = m }}
1698+--       Z := Z + X
1699+--                   {{ Z = (Y+1)*m /\ X = m }};
1700+--       Y := Y + 1
1701+--                   {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m }}
1702+--     end
1703+--   {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m /\ ~(Y <> X) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1704+--   {{ Z = m*m }}
1705+
1706+-- This new loop invariant makes the proof go through: all three conditions
1707+-- are easy to check.
1708+
1709+-- It is worth comparing the postcondition `Z = m*m` and the `Z = Y*m`
1710+-- conjunct of the loop invariant. It is often the case that one has to
1711+-- replace parameters with variables — or with expressions involving both
1712+-- variables and parameters, like `m - Y` — when going from postconditions to
1713+-- loop invariants.
1714+
1715+-- Note to developers:
1716+--     `HIDE: the more complicated version from 2012's class
1717+--
1718+--     Here is a program that squares X by repeated addition:
1719+--     [[
1720+--       X := n;
1721+--       Y := X;
1722+--       Z := 0;
1723+--       while Y <> 0 do
1724+--         Z := Z + X;
1725+--         Y := Y - 1
1726+--       end
1727+--     ]]
1728+--
1729+--       Bob's simpler loop invariant for squaring [square_dec]:
1730+--       (a very similar invariant given as solution in 2011 final; exercise 3)
1731+--
1732+--     [[
1733+--       {{ True }}
1734+--       X := n;
1735+--       {{ X = n }}
1736+--       Y := X;
1737+--       {{ X = n /\ Y = n }}
1738+--       Z := 0;
1739+--       {{ X = n /\ Y = n /\ Z = 0}} ->>
1740+--       {{ Z + X * Y = n * n }}
1741+--       while Y <> 0 do
1742+--         {{ Z + X * Y = n * n /\ (Y <> 0)}} ->>
1743+--         {{ Z + X + X * (Y - 1) = n * n }}
1744+--         Z := Z + X;
1745+--         {{ Z + X * (Y - 1) = n * n }}
1746+--         Y := Y - 1
1747+--         {{ Z + X * Y = n * n }}
1748+--       end
1749+--       {{ Z + X * Y = n * n /\ ~(Y <> 0)}} ->>
1750+--       {{ Z = n * n }}
1751+--     ]]
1752+--
1753+--     The other loop invariant [square_dec']:
1754+--     [[
1755+--       {{ True }}
1756+--       X := n;
1757+--       {{ X = n }}
1758+--       Y := X;
1759+--       {{ X = n /\ Y = n }}
1760+--       Z := 0;
1761+--       {{ X = n /\ Y = n /\ Z = 0}} ->>
1762+--       {{ Z = X * (X - Y) /\ X = n /\ Y <= X }}
1763+--       while Y <> 0 do
1764+--         {{ Z = X * (X - Y) /\ X = n /\ Y <= X /\ (Y <> 0)}} ->>
1765+--         {{ Z + X = X * (X - (Y - 1)) /\ X = n /\ (Y - 1) <= X }}
1766+--         Z := Z + X;
1767+--         {{ Z = X * (X - (Y - 1)) /\ X = n /\ (Y - 1) <= X }}
1768+--         Y := Y - 1
1769+--         {{ Z = X * (X - Y) /\ X = n /\ Y <= X }}
1770+--       end
1771+--       {{ Z = X * (X - Y) /\ X = n /\ Y <= X /\ ~(Y <> 0)}} ->>
1772+--       {{ Z = n * n }}
1773+--     ]]`
1774+
1775+-- ### Exercise: Factorial
1776+
1777+-- Note to developers (before next release):
1778+--     Move this later? Might be harder than some of the others.
1779+
1780+-- Note to developers:
1781+--     `HIDE: LY: Many are tempted to use division in their propositions here,
1782+--     with the loop invariant [Y = m!/X!].
1783+--     Informally, such a decorated program can be correct if we assume
1784+--     they use real division (in Q or R). The issue is that formally in Rocq,
1785+--     the notation / is also in scope and means integer division, so a pedantic
1786+--     interpretation would mark those answers wrong, even though that is most
1787+--     likely *not* what students intended (thus making the grading unfair).
1788+--     Should we explicitly forbid use of division for this exercise?
1789+--     (I added a note to that effect in the problem statement).
1790+--
1791+--     MRC'20: I strengthened your note so that it explicitly advises
1792+--     against division (and subtraction).`
1793+
1794+-- ### Exercise (4 stars): factorial_correct (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1795+
1796+-- Recall that `n!` denotes the factorial of `n` (i.e., `n! =
1797+-- 1*2*...*n`). We
1798+-- can define the factorial function recursively in Lean as follows:
1799+
1800+def fact : Nat → Nat
1801+  | 0 => 1
1802+  | Nat.succ n => Nat.succ n * fact n
1803+
1804+#eval fact 5
1805+
1806+-- First, write the Imp program `factorial` that calculates the factorial of
1807+-- the number initially stored in the variable `X` and puts it in the variable
1808+-- `Y`.
1809+
1810+-- Using your definition `factorial` and `slowAssignmentDec` as a guide, write
1811+-- a formal decorated program `factorialDec` that implements the factorial
1812+-- function. Ordinary Lean functions such as `fact` can be applied directly to
1813+-- Imp variables inside assertions.
1814+
1815+-- Fill in the blanks and finish the proof of correctness. Bear in mind that
1816+-- we are working with natural numbers, for which both division and
1817+-- subtraction can behave differently than with real numbers. Excluding both
1818+-- operations from your loop invariant is advisable!
1819+
1820+-- Then state a theorem named `factorial_correct` that says `factorialDec` is
1821+-- correct, and prove the theorem. If all goes well, `verify` will leave you
1822+-- with just two subgoals, each of which requires establishing some
1823+-- mathematical property of `fact`, rather than proving anything about your
1824+-- program.
1825+
1826+-- Hint: if those two subgoals become tedious to prove, give some thought to
1827+-- how you could restate your assertions such that the mathematical operations
1828+-- are more amenable to manipulation in Lean. For example, recall that
1829+-- `1 + ...` is easier to work with than `... + 1`.
1830+
1831+def factorialDec (m : Nat) : Decorated := ({
1832+  pre := ({{ X = m }})
1833+  body := dcom {
1834+    ->> {{ 1 * fact X = fact m }}
1835+    Y := 1 {{ Y * fact X = fact m }};
1836+    while (X ≠ 0) do
1837+      {{ Y * fact X = fact m ∧ ¬ X = 0 }}
1838+      ->> {{ (Y * X) * fact (X - 1) = fact m }}
1839+      Y := Y * X {{ Y * fact (X - 1) = fact m }};
1840+      X := X - 1 {{ Y * fact X = fact m }}
1841+    end
1842+      {{ Y * fact X = fact m ∧ X = 0 }}
1843+    ->> {{ Y = fact m }}
1844+  }
1845+})
1846+
1847+theorem fact_sub_one (m : Nat) (h : m ≠ 0) :
1848+    m * fact (m - 1) = fact m := by
1849+  all_goals
1850+    sorry
1851+
1852+theorem factorial_correct (m : Nat) :
1853+    (factorialDec m).OuterTripleValid := by
1854+  all_goals
1855+    sorry
1856+
1857+-- Note to developers:
1858+--     HIDE: MRC'20: That's not really an Imp program though: it is a schema
1859+--     for an Imp program. `m` is not an Imp variable nor a constant. BCP 21:
1860+--     But we do that all over the place, no?
1861+--
1862+--     `HIDE: LY: I saw one submission for [factorial_dec] use a program
1863+--     like that instead of the one already given by the informal
1864+--     exercise. I accepted it because the exercise does not require to
1865+--     reuse the given program, and we did not strictly define what it
1866+--     means to "implement" factorial in Imp.  This other one "implements"
1867+--     factorial in the same way two_loops_dec "implements" the sum (a + b
1868+--     + c).`
1869+
1870+-- ### Exercise: Minimum
1871+
1872+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): minimum_correct (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1873+
1874+-- Fill in decorations for the following program and prove them correct. As
1875+-- with `factorial`, be careful about mathematical reasoning involving natural
1876+-- numbers, especially subtraction.
1877+
1878+-- Lean functions can be applied directly inside assertions. For example, the
1879+-- minimum of `a` and `b` can be written `Nat.min a b`.
1880+
1881+-- Note to developers:
1882+--     HIDE: MRC'20: It bothers me a bit that the `&&` in the guard below
1883+--     becomes a `/\` in the assertion. We've never explained that it's okay
1884+--     to do a translation like that.
1885+
1886+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2025):
1887+--     `Maybe we should write /\ in assertions??`
1888+
1889+def minimumDec (a b : Nat) : Decorated where
1890+  pre := ({{ True }})
1891+  body := dcom {
1892+    ->> {{ ({{ 0 + Nat.min a b = Nat.min a b }}) }}
1893+    X := ~(Aexp.num a) {{
1894+      ({{ 0 + Nat.min X b = Nat.min a b }})
1895+    }};
1896+    Y := ~(Aexp.num b) {{
1897+      ({{ 0 + Nat.min X Y = Nat.min a b }})
1898+    }};
1899+    Z := 0 {{
1900+      ({{ Z + Nat.min X Y = Nat.min a b }})
1901+    }};
1902+    while (X ≠ 0 ∧ Y ≠ 0) do
1903+      {{ ({{
1904+        Z + Nat.min X Y = Nat.min a b ∧ (¬ X = 0 ∧ ¬ Y = 0)
1905+      }}) }}
1906+      ->> {{ ({{
1907+        Z + 1 + Nat.min (X - 1) (Y - 1) = Nat.min a b
1908+      }}) }}
1909+      X := X - 1 {{
1910+        ({{
1911+          Z + 1 + Nat.min X (Y - 1) = Nat.min a b
1912+        }})
1913+      }};
1914+      Y := Y - 1 {{
1915+        ({{ Z + 1 + Nat.min X Y = Nat.min a b }})
1916+      }};
1917+      Z := Z + 1 {{
1918+        ({{ Z + Nat.min X Y = Nat.min a b }})
1919+      }}
1920+    end
1921+      {{ ({{
1922+        Z + Nat.min X Y = Nat.min a b ∧
1923+        ¬ (¬ X = 0 ∧ ¬ Y = 0)
1924+      }}) }}
1925+    ->> {{ Z = Nat.min a b }}
1926+  }
1927+
1928+-- Note to developers:
1929+--     HIDE: BCP 21: I'm sure there is a more elegant proof of this!!
1930+
1931+theorem minimum_correct (a b : Nat) :
1932+    (minimumDec a b).OuterTripleValid := by
1933+  all_goals
1934+    sorry
1935+
1936+-- Note to developers:
1937+--     `HIDE: LY: in this exercise, many end up writing the following implication
1938+--     after the while line:
1939+--
1940+--       {{ Z = min a b - min X Y /\ ... }} ->>
1941+--       {{ Z+1 = min a b - min (X-1) (Y-1) /\ ... }}
1942+--
1943+--     that is invalid if you interpret [-] pedantically as [sub : nat ->
1944+--     nat -> nat], which takes nonnegative values only. But if we are
1945+--     more generous and interpret these informal proofs in more intuitive
1946+--     domains (Z, Q, or R), then these proofs look fine. I made the
1947+--     former choice in my grading because I assume at this point they
1948+--     should know to be careful around [-] with [nat].  BCP 21: Should be
1949+--     fixed now that the proofs are formal! :-)`
1950+
1951+-- ### Exercise: Two Loops
1952+
1953+-- Note to developers:
1954+--     HIDE: Taken from midterm 2, 2012
1955+
1956+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): two_loops ⭐⭐⭐
1957+
1958+-- Here is a pretty inefficient way of adding 3 numbers:
1959+
1960+--   X := 0;
1961+--   Y := 0;
1962+--   Z := c;
1963+--   while X <> a do
1964+--     X := X + 1;
1965+--     Z := Z + 1
1966+--   end;
1967+--   while Y <> b do
1968+--     Y := Y + 1;
1969+--     Z := Z + 1
1970+--   end
1971+
1972+-- Show that it does what it should by completing the following decorated
1973+-- program.
1974+
1975+def twoLoopsDec (a b c : Nat) : Decorated where
1976+  pre := ({{ True }})
1977+  body := dcom {
1978+    ->> {{ ({{ c = 0 + c ∧ 0 = 0 }}) }}
1979+    X := 0 {{ ({{ c = X + c ∧ 0 = 0 }}) }};
1980+    Y := 0 {{ ({{ c = X + c ∧ Y = 0 }}) }};
1981+    Z := ~(Aexp.num c) {{
1982+      ({{ Z = X + c ∧ Y = 0 }})
1983+    }};
1984+    (while (X ≠ ~(Aexp.num a)) do
1985+      {{ ({{ (Z = X + c ∧ Y = 0) ∧ ¬ X = a }}) }}
1986+      ->> {{ ({{ Z + 1 = X + 1 + c ∧ Y = 0 }}) }}
1987+      X := X + 1 {{
1988+        ({{ Z + 1 = X + c ∧ Y = 0 }})
1989+      }};
1990+      Z := Z + 1 {{ ({{ Z = X + c ∧ Y = 0 }}) }}
1991+    end
1992+      {{ ({{ (Z = X + c ∧ Y = 0) ∧ X = a }}) }}
1993+    ->> {{ ({{ Z = a + Y + c }}) }});
1994+    while (Y ≠ ~(Aexp.num b)) do
1995+      {{ ({{ Z = a + Y + c ∧ ¬ Y = b }}) }}
1996+      ->> {{ ({{ Z + 1 = a + Y + 1 + c }}) }}
1997+      Y := Y + 1 {{ ({{ Z + 1 = a + Y + c }}) }};
1998+      Z := Z + 1 {{ ({{ Z = a + Y + c }}) }}
1999+    end
2000+      {{ ({{ Z = a + Y + c ∧ Y = b }}) }}
2001+    ->> {{ Z = a + b + c }}
2002+  }
2003+
2004+theorem two_loops (a b c : Nat) :
2005+    (twoLoopsDec a b c).OuterTripleValid := by
2006+  all_goals
2007+    sorry
2008+
2009+-- Solution:
2010+-- [[
2011+--     {{ True }} ->>
2012+--     {{ c = 0 + c /\ 0 = 0 }}
2013+--   X := 0;
2014+--     {{ c = X + c /\ 0 = 0 }}
2015+--   Y := 0;
2016+--     {{ c = X + c /\ Y = 0 }}
2017+--   Z := c;
2018+--     {{ Z = X + c /\ Y = 0 }}
2019+--   while X <> a do
2020+--       {{ Z = X + c /\ Y = 0 /\ X <> a }} ->>
2021+--       {{ Z + 1 = X + 1 + c /\ Y = 0 }}
2022+--     X := X + 1;
2023+--       {{ Z + 1 = X + c /\ Y = 0 }}
2024+--     Z := Z + 1
2025+--       {{ Z = X + c /\ Y = 0 }}
2026+--   end;
2027+--     {{ Z = X + c /\ Y = 0 /\ ~(X <> a) }} ->>
2028+--     {{ Z = a + Y + c }}
2029+--   while Y <> b do
2030+--       {{ Z = a + Y + c /\ Y <> b }} ->>
2031+--       {{ Z + 1 = a + Y + 1 + c }}
2032+--     Y := Y + 1;
2033+--       {{ Z + 1 = a + Y + c }}
2034+--     Z := Z + 1
2035+--       {{ Z = a + Y + c }}
2036+--   end
2037+--     {{ Z = a + Y + c /\ ~(Y <> b) }} ->>
2038+--     {{ Z = a + b + c }}
2039+-- ]]
2040+
2041+-- Another solution follows.  It doesn't require carrying an additional
2042+-- [Y = 0] conjunct through the first loop, but instead carries an
2043+-- additional [ + Y] term through it.
2044+
2045+-- [[
2046+--       {{ True }} ->>
2047+--         {{ c = 0 + 0 + c }}
2048+--     X := 0;
2049+--         {{ c = X + 0 + c }}
2050+--     Y := 0;
2051+--         {{ c = X + Y + c }}
2052+--     Z := c;
2053+--         {{ Z = X + Y + c }}
2054+--     while X <> a do
2055+--         {{ Z = X + Y + c /\ X <> a }} ->>
2056+--         {{ Z + 1 = (X + 1) + Y + c }}
2057+--       X := X + 1;
2058+--         {{ Z + 1 = X + Y + c }}
2059+--       Z := Z + 1
2060+--         {{ Z = X + Y + c }}
2061+--     end;
2062+--       {{ Z = X + Y + c /\ ~(X <> a) }} ->>
2063+--       {{ Z = a + Y + c }}
2064+--     while Y <> b do
2065+--         {{ Z = a + Y + c /\ (Y <> b) }} ->>
2066+--         {{ Z + 1 = a + (Y + 1) + c }}
2067+--       Y := Y + 1;
2068+--         {{ Z + 1 = a + Y + c }}
2069+--       Z := Z + 1
2070+--         {{ Z = a + Y + c }}
2071+--     end
2072+--       {{ Z = a + Y + c /\ ~(Y <> b) }} ->>
2073+--       {{ Z = a + b + c }}
2074+-- ]]
2075+

2083+--         Y := 1;
2084+--         Z := 1;
2085+--         while X <> W do
2086+--           Z := 2 * Z;
2087+--           Y := Y + Z;
2088+--           X := X + 1
2089+--         end
2090+--           {{ Y = 2 ^ (W + 1) - 1 }}
2091+--     ]]

2096+-- ### Exercise (4 stars): dpow2 ⭐⭐⭐⭐
2097+
2098+-- Here is a program that computes the series:
2099+-- `1 + 2 + 2^2 + ... + 2^m = 2^(m+1) - 1`
2100+
2101+--   X := 0;
2102+--   Y := 1;
2103+--   Z := 1;
2104+--   while X <> m do
2105+--     Z := 2 * Z;
2106+--     Y := Y + Z;
2107+--     X := X + 1
2108+--   end
2109+
2110+-- Turn this into a decorated program and prove it correct.
2111+
2112+def pow2 : Nat → Nat
2113+  | 0 => 1
2114+  | Nat.succ n => 2 * pow2 n
2115+
2116+def dpow2Dec (n : Nat) : Decorated where
2117+  pre := ({{ True }})
2118+  body := dcom {
2119+    ->> {{ ({{
2120+      1 = pow2 (0 + 1) - 1 ∧ 1 = pow2 0
2121+    }}) }}
2122+    X := 0 {{
2123+      ({{ 1 = pow2 (X + 1) - 1 ∧ 1 = pow2 X }})
2124+    }};
2125+    Y := 1 {{
2126+      ({{ Y = pow2 (X + 1) - 1 ∧ 1 = pow2 X }})
2127+    }};
2128+    Z := 1 {{
2129+      ({{ Y = pow2 (X + 1) - 1 ∧ Z = pow2 X }})
2130+    }};
2131+    while (X ≠ ~(Aexp.num n)) do
2132+      {{ ({{
2133+        (Y = pow2 (X + 1) - 1 ∧ Z = pow2 X) ∧ ¬ X = n
2134+      }}) }}
2135+      ->> {{ ({{
2136+        Y + 2 * Z = pow2 (X + 2) - 1 ∧
2137+        2 * Z = pow2 (X + 1)
2138+      }}) }}
2139+      Z := 2 * Z {{
2140+        ({{
2141+          Y + Z = pow2 (X + 2) - 1 ∧ Z = pow2 (X + 1)
2142+        }})
2143+      }};
2144+      Y := Y + Z {{
2145+        ({{
2146+          Y = pow2 (X + 2) - 1 ∧ Z = pow2 (X + 1)
2147+        }})
2148+      }};
2149+      X := X + 1 {{
2150+        ({{
2151+          Y = pow2 (X + 1) - 1 ∧ Z = pow2 X
2152+        }})
2153+      }}
2154+    end
2155+      {{ ({{
2156+        (Y = pow2 (X + 1) - 1 ∧ Z = pow2 X) ∧ X = n
2157+      }}) }}
2158+    ->> {{ Y = pow2 (n + 1) - 1 }}
2159+  }
2160+
2161+-- Some lemmas that you may find useful...
2162+
2163+theorem pow2_add_one (n : Nat) :
2164+    pow2 (n + 1) = pow2 n + pow2 n := by
2165+  sorry
2166+
2167+theorem one_le_pow2 (n : Nat) : 1 ≤ pow2 n := by
2168+  sorry
2169+
2170+-- The main correctness theorem:
2171+
2172+theorem dpow2_down_correct (n : Nat) :
2173+    (dpow2Dec n).OuterTripleValid := by
2174+  all_goals
2175+    sorry
