2177+-- Note to developers:
2178+--     `HIDE: Another (very) good exercise from 09-mid2 -- just needs typeset
2179+--
2180+--     The notion of weakest precondition has a natural dual : given a
2181+--     precondition and a command, we can ask what is the strongest
2182+--     postcondition of the command with respect to the
2183+--     precondition. Formally, we can define it like this:
2184+--
2185+--     Q is the strongest postcondition of c for P if:
2186+--
2187+--     (a) {{P}} c {{Q}}, and
2188+--
2189+--     (b) if Q′ is an assertion such that {{P}}c{{Q′}},
2190+--         then Q st implies Q′ st, for all states st.
2191+--
2192+--     Q is the strongest (most difficult to satisfy) assertion that is
2193+--     guaranteed to hold after c if P holds before. For example, the
2194+--     strongest postcondition of the command skip with respect to the
2195+--     precondition Y = 1 is Y = 1. Similarly, the postcondition in...
2196+--
2197+--              {{ Y = y }}
2198+--                if !Y === A0 then X := A0 else Y := !Y *** A2
2199+--              {{ (Y = y = X = 0) ∨ (Y = 2*y ∧ y <> 0) }}
2200+--
2201+--     ...is the strongest one.
2202+--
2203+--     Complete each of the following Hoare triples with the strongest
2204+--     postcondition for the given command and precondition.
2205+--
2206+--     (a) {{Y=1}} X:=!Y+++A1 {{?}}
2207+--     (b) {{True}} X:=A5 {{?}}
2208+--     (c) {{ True }} skip {{ ? }}
2209+--     (d) {{ True }} while true do skip {{ ? }}
2210+--     (e) {{ X = x ∧ Y = y }}
2211+--         while BNot (!X === A0) do (
2212+--                         Y := !Y +++ A2;
2213+--                         X := !X --- A1
2214+--                       )
2215+--         {{ ? }}`
2216+
2217+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): fib_eqn (Advanced) ⭐⭐
2218+
2219+-- The Fibonacci function is characterized by the equations
2220+
2221+--   fib 0 = 1
2222+--   fib 1 = 1
2223+--   fib (n + 2) = fib (n + 1) + fib n
2224+
2225+-- This recurrence can be defined structurally in Lean as follows:
2226+
2227+def fib : Nat → Nat
2228+  | 0 => 1
2229+  | Nat.succ 0 => 1
2230+  | Nat.succ (Nat.succ n) => fib (Nat.succ n) + fib n
2231+
2232+-- Prove that `fib` satisfies the following equation. You will need this as a
2233+-- lemma in the next exercise.
2234+
2235+theorem fib_eqn (n : Nat) (h : n > 0) :
2236+    fib n + fib (Nat.pred n) = fib (1 + n) := by
2237+  all_goals
2238+    sorry
2239+
2240+-- ### Exercise (4 stars): fib (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
2241+
2242+-- The following Imp program leaves the value of `fib n` in the variable `Y`
2243+-- when it terminates:
2244+
2245+--   X := 1;
2246+--   Y := 1;
2247+--   Z := 1;
2248+--   while X <> 1 + n do
2249+--     T := Z;
2250+--     Z := Z + Y;
2251+--     Y := T;
2252+--     X := 1 + X
2253+--   end
2254+
2255+-- Fill in the following definition of `dfib` and prove that it satisfies this
2256+-- specification:
2257+
2258+--   {{ True }} dfib {{ Y = fib n }}
2259+
2260+-- Ordinary Lean function application can be used in the assertions. If all
2261+-- goes well, your proof will be very brief.
2262+
2263+def T : Ident := "T"
2264+
2265+def dfib (n : Nat) : Decorated where
2266+  pre := ({{ True }})
2267+  body :=
2268+    let init : Assertion :=
2269+      (fun _ =>
2270+        1 = fib 0 ∧ 1 = fib (Nat.pred 0) ∧ 1 > 0)
2271+    let afterX : Assertion :=
2272+      (fun st =>
2273+        1 = fib (st X) ∧
2274+        1 = fib (Nat.pred (st X)) ∧ st X > 0)
2275+    let afterY : Assertion :=
2276+      (fun st =>
2277+        1 = fib (st X) ∧
2278+        st Y = fib (Nat.pred (st X)) ∧ st X > 0)
2279+    let inv : Assertion :=
2280+      (fun st =>
2281+        st Z = fib (st X) ∧
2282+        st Y = fib (Nat.pred (st X)) ∧ st X > 0)
2283+    let guardedInv : Assertion :=
2284+      (fun st =>
2285+        st Z = fib (st X) ∧ st Y = fib (Nat.pred (st X)) ∧
2286+        st X > 0 ∧ st X ≠ 1 + n)
2287+    let bodyPre : Assertion :=
2288+      (fun st =>
2289+        st Z + st Y = fib (1 + st X) ∧
2290+        st Z = fib (Nat.pred (1 + st X)) ∧ 1 + st X > 0)
2291+    let afterT : Assertion :=
2292+      (fun st =>
2293+        st Z + st Y = fib (1 + st X) ∧
2294+        st T = fib (Nat.pred (1 + st X)) ∧ 1 + st X > 0)
2295+    let afterZ : Assertion :=
2296+      (fun st =>
2297+        st Z = fib (1 + st X) ∧
2298+        st T = fib (Nat.pred (1 + st X)) ∧ 1 + st X > 0)
2299+    let afterYBody : Assertion :=
2300+      (fun st =>
2301+        st Z = fib (1 + st X) ∧
2302+        st Y = fib (Nat.pred (1 + st X)) ∧ 1 + st X > 0)
2303+    let exit : Assertion :=
2304+      (fun st =>
2305+        st Z = fib (st X) ∧ st Y = fib (Nat.pred (st X)) ∧
2306+        st X > 0 ∧ st X = 1 + n)
2307+    dcom {
2308+      ->> {{ init }}
2309+      X := 1 {{ afterX }};
2310+      Y := 1 {{ afterY }};
2311+      Z := 1 {{ inv }};
2312+      while (X ≠ ~(Aexp.num (1 + n))) do
2313+        {{ guardedInv }}
2314+        ->> {{ bodyPre }}
2315+        T := Z {{ afterT }};
2316+        Z := Z + Y {{ afterZ }};
2317+        Y := T {{ afterYBody }};
2318+        X := 1 + X {{ inv }}
2319+      end
2320+        {{ exit }}
2321+      ->> {{ Y = fib n }}
2322+    }
2323+
2324+theorem dfib_correct (n : Nat) :
2325+    (dfib n).OuterTripleValid := by
2326+  all_goals
2327+    sorry
2328+
2329+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2021):
2330+--     This exercise should really be expanded into its own whole section.
2331+--     Moreover, there is a proposal to make the decorations in Hoare look
2332+--     more like the decorations earlier in the present chapter. All three
2333+--     should be aligned.
2334+
2335+-- ### Exercise (5 stars): improve_dcom (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
2336+
2337+-- The formal decorated programs defined above are intended to look as similar
2338+-- as possible to the informal ones defined earlier. If we drop this
2339+-- requirement, we can eliminate almost all annotations, just requiring final
2340+-- postconditions and loop invariants to be provided explicitly. Do this —
2341+-- i.e., define a new version of `DCom` with as few annotations as possible
2342+-- and adapt the rest of the formal development leading up to the
2343+-- `verification_correct` theorem.
2344+
2345+namespace SparseAnnotations
2346+
2347+/- (This solution also allows optional post-condition
2348+assertions at any point, since these are quite useful in
2349+practice when debugging the results of automated VC
2350+solvers.) -/
2351+
2352+inductive DCom where
2353+  | skip
2354+  | seq (first second : DCom)
2355+  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp)
2356+  | cond (b : Bexp) (thenBranch elseBranch : DCom)
2357+  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (invariant : Assertion) (body : DCom)
2358+  | assert (assertion : Assertion)
2359+
2360+structure Decorated where
2361+  pre : Assertion
2362+  body : DCom
2363+  post : Assertion
2364+
2365+declare_syntax_cat sparse_dcom
2366+
2367+syntax:max "(" sparse_dcom ")" : sparse_dcom
2368+syntax:max "skip" : sparse_dcom
2369+syntax:max ident " := " imp_aexp : sparse_dcom
2370+syntax:20 sparse_dcom:21 ";" ppLine
2371+  sparse_dcom:20 : sparse_dcom
2372+syntax:max "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "then" ppLine
2373+  sparse_dcom ppLine "else" ppLine sparse_dcom ppLine
2374+  "end" : sparse_dcom
2375+syntax:max "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "do" ppLine
2376+  "{{" term "}}" ppLine sparse_dcom ppLine
2377+  "end" : sparse_dcom
2378+syntax:max "assert" " {{" term "}}" : sparse_dcom
2379+
2380+syntax:min "sdcom" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine
2381+  sparse_dcom ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
2382+
2383+macro_rules
2384+  | `(sdcom { ($body:sparse_dcom) }) =>
2385+      `(sdcom { $body })
2386+  | `(sdcom { skip }) =>
2387+      `(DCom.skip)
2388+  | `(sdcom { $x:ident := $a:imp_aexp }) =>
2389+      `(DCom.asgn $x (aexp { $a }))
2390+  | `(sdcom { $d1:sparse_dcom; $d2:sparse_dcom }) =>
2391+      `(DCom.seq (sdcom { $d1 }) (sdcom { $d2 }))
2392+  | `(sdcom {
2393+        if ($b:imp_bexp) then
2394+          $d1:sparse_dcom
2395+        else
2396+          $d2:sparse_dcom
2397+        end
2398+      }) =>
2399+      `(DCom.cond (bexp { $b })
2400+        (sdcom { $d1 }) (sdcom { $d2 }))
2401+  | `(sdcom {
2402+        while ($b:imp_bexp) do
2403+          {{ $inv }}
2404+          $body:sparse_dcom
2405+        end
2406+      }) =>
2407+      `(DCom.whileDo (bexp { $b }) ({{ $inv }})
2408+        (sdcom { $body }))
2409+  | `(sdcom { assert {{ $p }} }) =>
2410+      `(DCom.assert ({{ $p }}))
2411+
2412+/- Here's how our decorated programs look now: -/
2413+
2414+def decWhile : Decorated where
2415+  pre := ({{ True }})
2416+  body := sdcom {
2417+    while (X ≠ 0) do
2418+      {{ True }}
2419+      X := X - 1
2420+    end
2421+  }
2422+  post := ({{ X = 0 }})
2423+
2424+/- It is easy to go from a `DCom` to a `Com` by erasing all
2425+annotations. -/
2426+
2427+def DCom.erase (d : DCom) : Com :=
2428+  match d with
2429+  | .skip => .skip
2430+  | .seq d1 d2 => .seq d1.erase d2.erase
2431+  | .asgn x a => .asgn x a
2432+  | .cond b d1 d2 => .cond b d1.erase d2.erase
2433+  | .whileDo b _ body => .whileDo b body.erase
2434+  | .assert _ => .skip
2435+
2436+/- We can express what it means for a decorated program to
2437+be correct as follows: -/
2438+
2439+def Decorated.OuterTripleValid (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
2440+  ValidHoareTriple dec.pre dec.body.erase dec.post
2441+
2442+/- This VC generator is derived from Mike Gordon,
2443+"Background reading on Hoare Logic,"
2444+https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/archive/mjcg/HL/Notes/Notes.pdf -/
2445+
2446+def DCom.awp (post : Assertion) (d : DCom) : Assertion :=
2447+  match d with
2448+  | .skip => post
2449+  | .seq d1 d2 => d1.awp (d2.awp post)
2450+  | .asgn x a => Assertion.sub x a post
2451+  | .cond b d1 d2 =>
2452+      fun st =>
2453+        (b.eval st = true ∧ d1.awp post st) ∨
2454+        (b.eval st = false ∧ d2.awp post st)
2455+  | .whileDo _ invariant _ => invariant
2456+  | .assert assertion => fun st => assertion st ∧ post st
2457+
2458+def DCom.VerificationConditions
2459+    (post : Assertion) (d : DCom) : Prop :=
2460+  match d with
2461+  | .seq d1 d2 =>
2462+      d1.VerificationConditions (d2.awp post) ∧
2463+      d2.VerificationConditions post
2464+  | .cond _ d1 d2 =>
2465+      d1.VerificationConditions post ∧
2466+      d2.VerificationConditions post
2467+  | .whileDo b invariant body =>
2468+      (∀ st, invariant st ∧ b.eval st ≠ true → post st) ∧
2469+      (∀ st, invariant st ∧ b.eval st = true →
2470+        body.awp invariant st) ∧
2471+      body.VerificationConditions invariant
2472+  | _ => True
2473+
2474+theorem vc_correct (d : DCom) (post : Assertion)
2475+    (hvc : d.VerificationConditions post) :
2476+    ValidHoareTriple (d.awp post) d.erase post := by
2477+  sorry
2478+
2479+def Decorated.VerificationConditions
2480+    (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
2481+  (dec.pre ->> dec.body.awp dec.post) ∧
2482+  dec.body.VerificationConditions dec.post
2483+
2484+theorem verification_correct (dec : Decorated)
2485+    (hvc : dec.VerificationConditions) :
2486+    dec.OuterTripleValid := by
2487+  sorry
2488+

2492+    decWhile.OuterTripleValid := by
2493+  sorry

2495+def swapDec (m n : Nat) : Decorated where
2496+  pre := ({{ X = m ∧ Y = n }})
2497+  body := sdcom {
2498+    X := X + Y;
2499+    Y := X - Y;
2500+    X := X - Y
2501+  }
2502+  post := ({{ X = n ∧ Y = m }})
2503+
2504+theorem swap_correct (m n : Nat) :
2505+    (swapDec m n).OuterTripleValid := by
2506+  sorry

2509+  pre := ({{ True }})
2510+  body := sdcom {
2511+    if (X ≤ Y) then
2512+      Z := Y - X
2513+    else
2514+      Z := X - Y
2515+    end
2516+  }
2517+  post := ({{ Z + X = Y ∨ Z + Y = X }})
2518+
2519+theorem if_minus_correct :
2520+    ifMinusDec.OuterTripleValid := by
2521+  sorry

2523+def ifMinusPlusDec : Decorated where

2525+  body := sdcom {
2526+    if (X ≤ Y) then
2527+      Z := Y - X
2528+    else
2529+      Y := X + Z
2530+    end
2531+  }
2532+  post := ({{ Y = X + Z }})

2538+def divModDec (a b : Nat) : Decorated where
2539+  pre := ({{ True }})
2540+  body := sdcom {
2541+    X := ~(Aexp.num a);
2542+    Y := 0;
2543+    while (~(Aexp.num b) ≤ X) do
2544+      {{ b * Y + X = a }}
2545+      X := X - ~(Aexp.num b);
2546+      Y := Y + 1
2547+    end
2548+  }
2549+  post := ({{ b * Y + X = a ∧ X < b }})

2556+  pre := ({{ X = m }})

2558+    while (2 ≤ X) do

2561+    end
2562+  }
2563+  post := ({{ X = parity m }})

2570+  pre := ({{ X = m }})
2571+  body := sdcom {
2572+    Z := 0;
2573+    while ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ X) do

2576+    end
2577+  }
2578+  post := ({{ Z * Z ≤ m ∧ m < (Z + 1) * (Z + 1) }})

2647+    while (Y ≠ ~(Aexp.num b)) do

2709+def T : Ident := "T"
2710+
2711+def dfib (n : Nat) : Decorated where
2712+  pre := ({{ True }})
2713+  body := sdcom {
2714+    X := 1;
2715+    Y := 1;
2716+    Z := 1;
2717+    while (X ≠ ~(Aexp.num (1 + n))) do
2718+      {{ Z = fib X ∧ Y = fib (Nat.pred X) ∧ X > 0 }}
2719+      T := Z;
2720+      Z := Z + Y;
2721+      Y := T;
2722+      X := 1 + X
2723+    end
2724+  }
2725+  post := ({{ Y = fib n }})

2727+theorem dfib_correct (n : Nat) :
2728+    (dfib n).OuterTripleValid := by
2729+  sorry
2730+
2731+
2732+end SparseAnnotations

2734+-- ## Weakest Preconditions (Optional)
2735+
2736+-- Note to developers:
2737+--     HIDE: BCP 21: We talked about moving this stuff to the HoareAsLogic
2738+--     chapter to lighten this chapter, but it fits awkwardly there, so I'm
2739+--     leaving it here. It's optional anyway. We might consider assigning one
2740+--     of the exercises as advanced-only though.
2741+
2742+-- Some preconditions are more interesting than others. For example, the Hoare
2743+-- triple
2744+
2745+--   {{ False }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
2746+
2747+-- is *not* very interesting: although it is perfectly valid, it tells us
2748+-- nothing useful. Since the precondition isn't satisfied by any state, it
2749+-- doesn't describe any situations where we can use the command `X := Y + 1`
2750+-- to achieve the postcondition `X <= 5`.
2751+
2752+-- By contrast,
2753+
2754+--   {{ Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0 }}  X := Y + 1 {{ X <= 5 }}
2755+
2756+-- has a useful precondition: it tells us that, if we can somehow create a
2757+-- situation in which we know that `Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0`, then running this
2758+-- command will produce a state satisfying the postcondition. However, this
2759+-- precondition is not as useful as it could be, because the `Z = 0` clause in
2760+-- the precondition actually has nothing to do with the postcondition
2761+-- `X <= 5`.
2762+
2763+-- The *most* useful precondition for this command is this one:
2764+
2765+--   {{ Y <= 4 }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
2766+
2767+-- The assertion `Y <= 4` is called the *weakest precondition* of `X := Y + 1`
2768+-- with respect to the postcondition `X <= 5`.
2769+
2770+-- Assertion `Y <= 4` is a *weakest precondition* of command `X := Y + 1` with
2771+-- respect to postcondition `X <= 5`. Think of *weakest* here as meaning
2772+-- "easiest to satisfy": a weakest precondition is one that as many states as
2773+-- possible can satisfy.
2774+
2775+-- `P` is a weakest precondition of command `c` for postcondition `Q` if
2776+
2777+-- - `P` is a precondition, that is, `{{P}} c {{Q}}`; and
2778+
2779+-- - `P` is at least as weak as all other preconditions, that is, if
2780+--   `{{P'}} c {{Q}}` then `P' ->> P`.
2781+
2782+-- Note that weakest preconditions need not be unique. For example, `Y <= 4`
2783+-- was a weakest precondition above, but so are the logically equivalent
2784+-- assertions `Y < 5`, `Y <= 2 * 2`, etc. It is easy to show that any two
2785+-- weakest preconditions `P` and `P'` of a command `c` with respect to
2786+-- postcondition `Q` are logically equivalent; that is, `P <<->> P'`.
2787+
2788+def IsWp (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
2789+  ValidHoareTriple P c Q ∧
2790+  ∀ P' : Assertion, ValidHoareTriple P' c Q → P' ->> P
2791+
2792+-- ### Exercise (1 star): wp ⭐
2793+
2794+-- What are weakest preconditions of the following commands for the following
2795+-- postconditions?
2796+
2797+--   1) {{ ? }}  skip  {{ X = 5 }}
2798+
2799+--   2) {{ ? }}  X := Y + Z {{ X = 5 }}
2800+
2801+--   3) {{ ? }}  X := Y  {{ X = Y }}
2802+
2803+--   4) {{ ? }}
2804+--    if X = 0 then Y := Z + 1 else Y := W + 2 end
2805+--    {{ Y = 5 }}
2806+
2807+--   5) {{ ? }}
2808+--    X := 5
2809+--    {{ X = 0 }}
2810+
2811+--   6) {{ ? }}
2812+--    while true do X := 0 end
2813+--    {{ X = 0 }}
2814+
2815+--   1) X = 5
2816+--   2) Y + Z = 5
2817+--   3) True
2818+--   4) (X = 0 /\ Z = 4) \/ (X <> 0 /\ W = 3)
2819+--   5) False
2820+--   6) True
2821+
2822+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): is_wp (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
2823+
2824+-- Prove formally, using the definition of `ValidHoareTriple`, that `Y <= 4`
2825+-- is indeed a weakest precondition of `X := Y + 1` with respect to
2826+-- postcondition `X <= 5`.
2827+
2828+theorem is_wp_example :
2829+    IsWp ({{ Y ≤ 4 }}) (imp {X := Y + 1;})
2830+      ({{ X ≤ 5 }}) := by
2831+  all_goals
2832+    sorry
2833+
2834+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_weakest (Advanced) ⭐⭐
2835+
2836+-- Show that the precondition in the rule `hoare_asgn` is in fact the weakest
2837+-- precondition.
2838+
2839+theorem hoare_asgn_weakest
2840+    (Q : Assertion) (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) :
2841+    IsWp (Assertion.sub x a Q) (imp {x := ~a;}) Q := by
2842+  all_goals
2843+    sorry
2844+
2845+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_havoc_weakest (Advanced) ⭐⭐
2846+
2847+-- Show that your `havoc_pre` function from the `himp_hoare` exercise in the
2848+-- Hoare chapter returns a weakest precondition.
2849+
2850+namespace Himp2
2851+
2852+theorem hoare_havoc_weakest (P Q : Assertion) (x : Ident)
2853+    (h : Himp.ValidHoareTriple P (Himp.Com.havoc x) Q) :
2854+    P ->> Himp.havoc_pre x Q := by
2855+  all_goals
2856+    sorry
2857+
2858+end Himp2

250+-- We make it a little easier to write Imp programs using normal constructors
251+-- (i.e., without notation), by using *implicit coercions*. In Lean, a `Coe`
252+-- instance tells the elaborator how to turn a value of one type into another
253+-- automatically:
254+
255+-- - `Coe Ident Aexp` lets us write a bare variable (an `Ident`) where an `Aexp`
256+--   is expected; the identifier is implicitly wrapped with `id`.
257+
258+-- - `OfNat Aexp n` lets us write a numeric literal where an `Aexp` is expected;
259+--   it is implicitly wrapped with `num`.
260+
261+-- - `Coe Bool Bexp` lets us write a boolean literal (`true`/`false`) where a
262+--   `Bexp` is expected; it is implicitly wrapped with `bool`.
263+
264+instance : Coe Ident Aexp where
265+  coe := .id
266+
267+instance (n : Nat) : OfNat Aexp n where
268+  ofNat := .num n
269+
270+instance : Coe Bool Bexp where
271+  coe := .bool
272+
273+-- With these coercions we can write `.plus 3 (.mult X 2)` instead of the
274+-- fully explicit `.plus (.num 3) (.mult (.id "X") (.num 2))`, and
275+-- `.and true (.not …)` instead of `.and (.bool true) (.not …)`. More readably
276+-- still, the concrete syntax from the Notations section lets us write these
277+-- examples directly:
278+
279+def example_aexp : Aexp := aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }
280+def example_bexp : Bexp := bexp { true ∧ ¬(X ≤ 4) }

250-/-- In Lean, "inversion" on `leq : f n ≤ 0`, where `f : Nat → Nat`,
251-  requires `generalizing e : f n = m`, since Lean does not perform
252-  the dependent case analysis automatically. `cases leq` will fail here.
253-  We want to keep the style of reasoning familiar to PL:
254-  "I know `h`; what must have been true for `h` to be true?"
255-  The technicality of needing to generalize hinders teaching and learning
256-  this style of reasoning for audiences new to proof assistants and logic.
257-  To solve this, we introduce and use the `inversion` tactic,
258-  which automatically generalizes varaibles, performs case analysis,
259-  and eliminates impossible subcases. -/

383-namespace Algebra
384-
385--- This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively in Lean to define
386--- mathematical structures that carry both operators and laws about how those
387--- operators interact. As a simple example, let's use a typeclass to define a
388--- *monoid*, a simple algebraic structure that includes four things:
389-
390--- - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
391-
392--- - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that combines two
393---   elements of type `α` into one,
394-
395--- - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call the "identity
396---   element", and
397-
398--- - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`, namely that:
399-
400---   - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
401---   - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗` is associative)
402-
403--- We can express these requirements in the form of a typeclass:
404-
405--- first we define a notation typeclass for our operator ⊗
406-class OpSet (α : Type) where
407-  op : α → α → α
408-
409-infixr:70 " ⊗ " => OpSet.op
410-
411-class Monoid (α : Type) extends (OpSet α) where
412-  id : α
413-  left_id : ∀ (x : α), id ⊗ x = x
414-  right_id : ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ id = x
415-  assoc : ∀ (x y z : α), x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
416-
417--- The `extends` keyword indicates that the `Monoid` typeclass extends the
418--- `OpSet` typeclass, which just defines a set with an operator and some
419--- notation for it. The `Monoid` typeclass "inherits" the fields of `OpSet`,
420--- similar to how a class would in an object-oriented language.
421-
422--- As one might expect, the `+` operator over `Nat`s forms a monoid, where `0`
423--- is the identity element. Note that we don't have to define `Nat`'s `OpSet`
424--- instance separately, we can define a single instance that implements both
425--- classes.
426-
427-instance : Monoid Nat where
428-  op := Nat.add
429-  id := 0
430-  left_id := by lia
431-  right_id := by lia
432-  assoc := by lia
433-

441-  id := (1)
442-  left_id := (by lia)
443-  right_id := (by lia)
444-  assoc := (by lia)
445-
446--- ### Exercise (1 star): ListMonoidAppend ⭐
447-
448--- There are also many monoids over other types. Most usefully in computer
449--- science, lists of any type also form a monoid, with `List.append` as the
450--- operator in question:
451-
452-instance {α : Type} : Monoid (List α) where
453-  op := List.append
454-  id := ([])
455-  left_id := (by simp)
456-  right_id := (by simp)
457-  assoc := (by simp)
458-
459--- In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can also prove some
460--- properties about monoids in general, just based on the laws defined on the
461--- typeclass. One simple theorem about monoids is that the identity element of
462--- a monoid is unique. That is, if we have two monoids over the same set with
463--- the same operator, their identity elements must also be the same:
464-
465-theorem id_unique {α : Type} {m₁ m₂ : Monoid α} (h : m₁.op = m₂.op) : m₁.id = m₂.id := by
466-  obtain @⟨op₁, id₁, left_id₁, right_id₁, assoc₁⟩ := m₁
467-  obtain @⟨op₂, id₂, left_id₂, right_id₂, assoc₂⟩ := m₂
468-  have h' : id₁ = id₂ := by
469-    -- this introduces a use of m₁'s operator
470-    rw [← left_id₁ id₂]
471-    -- we use our hypothesis to rewrite m₁'s operator into m₂'s
472-    rw [h]
473-    -- then, we can use m₂'s right id
474-    rw [right_id₂]
475-  -- the goal `m₁.id = m₂.id` is equivalent with `id₁ = id₂` even though it displays `Monoid.id = Monoid.id`
476-  exact h'
477-
478--- In the above proof, we can destructure the monoid instances `m₁` and `m₂`
479--- with the `obtain` tactic we saw in the Logic chapter. When we do so
480--- however, because these are class instances instead of normal structures, we
481--- preface our tuple with the `@` symbol. When stepping through the above
482--- proof, if the notation is confusing to you, remember that you can set
483--- `set_option pp.all true` or `set_option pp.explicit true` to make Lean show
484--- you more clearly what is going on. For example, the goal is displayed as
485--- `Monoid.id = Monoid.id` since the instances `m₁` and `m₂` are implicit
486--- arguments to `Monoid.id`. Setting `pp.explicit true` displays the goal as
487--- `@Eq α (@Monoid.id α m₁) (@Monoid.id α m₂)`.
488-
489--- A *group* is a special kind of monoid with an *inverse* operation `inv`,
490--- which has the property that `∀ x, inv x ⊗ x = id = x ⊗ inv x`. We can
491--- extend the definition of a `Monoid` to capture this new feature:
492-
493-class Group (α : Type) extends (Monoid α) where
494-  inv : α → α
495-  left_inv : ∀ (x : α), inv x ⊗ x = id
496-  right_inv: ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ inv x = id
497-

499--- operation on the natural numbers such that
500--- `∀ x, x + inv x = 0 = inv x + x`, for example. However, addition does form
501--- a group over the integers:

603+--     `example (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m a = m[a] := by
604+--       -- simp -- doesn't work (infinite loop)
605+--       -- dsimp -- doesn't work (nothing happens)
606+--       -- rw [apply_eq_getElem] -- doesn't work: The pattern to be substituted is a metavariable (`?m ?a`) in this equality: ?m ?a = ?m[?a]

610+--     with `trace.Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite` enabled and specifying maxSteps
611+--     to simp, we can track what's going on:
612+--
613+--     `[Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
614+--           m a
615+--         ==>
616+--           m[a]
617+--     [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
618+--           m[a]
619+--         ==>
620+--           (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]
621+--     [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
622+--           (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]
623+--         ==>
624+--           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]
625+--     [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
626+--           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]
627+--         ==>
628+--           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m)))[a]
629+--     [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
630+--           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m)))[a]
631+--         ==>...`
632+--
633+--     So I think the issue here is that the LHS m a is too board, causing
634+--     this lemma repeating itself. First we have `m a => m[a], but m[a]` is
635+--     defeq to (MyGetElem.getElem m) a, and nevertheless we require m to be a
636+--     TotalMap, a TotalMap is defeq to α → β. So this lemma applies again --
637+--     `(MyGetElem.getElem m) a => (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]` which is
638+--     `(MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]` and keep going.
